lessons.plain: A cloud deployment model describes who owns the computers your systems run on and who else shares them. Public cloud means renting space on a big provider's shared machines. Private cloud means machines used by only your organization. Hybrid cloud links private and public so they work as one setup. Multi-cloud means using two or more public providers at once. Think of housing: renting a flat in a large building (public), owning a house (private), owning a house while renting a holiday flat for busy summers (hybrid), or renting flats from two different landlords (multi-cloud). Each choice fits a different need.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small online shop has no IT staff, no servers, and traffic that triples every December. Would it be better off owning its own servers or renting shared ones from a large provider? Why?
lessons.teach:
A deployment model is the answer to two questions: who owns the infrastructure, and who shares it. A public cloud is run by a provider that rents shared computing, storage, and networking to many customers, called tenants. You pay as you go, which is an operating expense rather than a large up-front capital expense, and you can scale quickly. A private cloud gives one organization dedicated infrastructure, either in its own data center or hosted for it alone. It offers the most control, which helps with data sovereignty (rules about where data must physically live), but you buy and run the capacity yourself. A hybrid cloud connects private and public environments so workloads and data can move between them; a common pattern is cloud bursting, where extra demand spills into public cloud during peaks. Multi-cloud means using two or more public providers, often to avoid vendor lock-in (being stuck with one provider's prices and services) or to use each provider's strengths. A community cloud is shared by organizations with similar requirements, such as several government agencies.

Worked example: a regional hospital must keep patient records on equipment it controls, but its appointment website spikes every flu season. Step one, list constraints: regulated records, seasonal web traffic. Step two, records point to private. Step three, spiky traffic points to public elasticity. Step four, the two must talk to each other. The fit is hybrid: records stay private, the website runs and scales in public cloud, connected securely.

A common mistake is treating hybrid and multi-cloud as the same thing. Hybrid mixes private with public; multi-cloud mixes public providers. Picking multi-cloud when hybrid was needed leaves the compliance problem unsolved. Picking multi-cloud without a clear reason multiplies the tools, skills, and data-transfer charges your team must manage, which slows operations and raises cost in a running system.

questions.prompt:
A mobile game studio runs all its servers on one public cloud provider (call it Provider A). It wants to use a machine-learning service that only Provider B offers. Leadership also worries that Provider A could raise prices and leave them with nowhere to go. The studio owns no data center, and no rule says where its data must physically live. The team works through the choice of deployment model:

Step 1: List the constraints. They want Provider B's unique service, they fear price dependence on Provider A, they have no data-location rules, and they own no hardware.
Step 2: With no data-location rules and no owned hardware, nothing points to a private cloud.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: The fit is multi-cloud. Game servers stay on Provider A, and the machine-learning work runs on Provider B.

Which statement correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Seasonal player spikes point to cloud bursting from a private environment into public cloud.
The fear of price increases points to buying dedicated hardware, so the studio controls its own costs.
Sharing infrastructure with other game studios that have similar needs points to a community cloud.
Wanting a second provider's strengths and avoiding vendor lock-in point to using two or more public providers.
questions.why: Multi-cloud means using two or more public providers, and the usual reasons are to use each provider's strengths and to avoid vendor lock-in, which are exactly the studio's two goals.

questions.prompt: Five regional credit unions all follow the same financial regulations. They want to share one cloud environment built to meet those common requirements, instead of each building its own. Which deployment model fits?
choices: Hybrid cloud
Public cloud
Community cloud
Multi-cloud
questions.why: A community cloud is shared by organizations with similar requirements, which describes credit unions that follow the same regulations.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm must keep customer claim files on equipment it controls. A consultant recommends spreading its workloads across two public cloud providers and calls this the right answer. What is the main problem with this advice?
choices: Multi-cloud requires a large up-front capital expense that public clouds avoid.
It mixes public providers only, so the files still are not on equipment the firm controls, and the compliance need is unsolved.
Two public providers count as a private cloud, so the firm would be paying for the same thing twice.
Multi-cloud always costs less than hybrid, so the firm would overspend by not choosing it sooner.
questions.why: Multi-cloud combines public providers, not private with public, so it does not keep the regulated files on controlled equipment. That is the mistake of confusing multi-cloud with hybrid.

questions.prompt: A new nonprofit has no IT staff and no money for large equipment purchases. Its volunteer sign-up site may grow quickly or stay small; nobody knows yet. It has no rules about where its data must live. Which deployment model best fits, and why?
choices: Private cloud, because dedicated infrastructure gives the most control over growth.
Public cloud, because pay-as-you-go turns costs into an operating expense and capacity can scale quickly.
Hybrid cloud, because the nonprofit needs to burst from its own data center during peaks.
Multi-cloud, because using two providers is the standard starting point for any new organization.
questions.why: Public cloud avoids up-front capital spending, charges as you go, and scales quickly. Nothing in the nonprofit's needs calls for owned hardware or a second provider.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between public, private, hybrid, and multi-cloud for a new workload, and name one tradeoff that comes with each choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start from the business constraints, not the technology. If the workload has no strict rules about where data lives and demand is unpredictable, public cloud fits: pay as you go and scale fast, but we share infrastructure and give up some control. If regulation or security needs full control, private cloud fits, but we pay up front and must run the capacity ourselves, so scaling is slower. If we have both needs, say regulated data plus spiky customer traffic, hybrid connects private and public so each part lands in the right place; the cost is the complexity of linking and securing two environments. Multi-cloud means using several public providers, useful to avoid lock-in or use one provider's special strength, but it multiplies tools, skills, and data-transfer charges. I also check not to confuse hybrid, which includes private, with multi-cloud, which is all public.
rubricPoints: Starts from business constraints such as compliance, demand pattern, and budget.
Defines public cloud as shared, provider-run, pay-as-you-go with less control.
Defines private cloud as dedicated, more control, higher up-front cost and slower scaling.
Describes hybrid as connected private and public, with integration complexity as the tradeoff.
Distinguishes multi-cloud (several public providers) from hybrid and names lock-in avoidance versus added complexity.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a deployment model is a scenario-matching skill best built by reasoning through exam-style workload descriptions, and no current mission or planned engine has learners pick a cloud model.

lessons.plain: Virtualization means using software to split one physical computer into several pretend computers, called virtual machines. Each one behaves like a complete machine with its own operating system, but they all share the same real processor, memory, and disks underneath. Think of an apartment building: one structure, many separate homes, each with its own locked door. Cloud providers rely on this trick. It lets them rent you a slice of a big server in minutes, pack many customers onto the same hardware safely, and move or copy your machine without touching anything physical.
lessons.guessPrompt: A physical server has 32 processor cores. If a cloud provider runs 16 virtual machines on it and gives each one 4 virtual processors, is that more or fewer processors than the server really has? What could go wrong if every machine got busy at once?
lessons.teach:
Virtualization is the use of software to present physical hardware as several independent virtual machines (VMs). The physical server is the host; each VM is a guest running its own operating system. The software layer that does the splitting is the hypervisor. A Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor runs directly on the hardware and is what cloud data centers use, because nothing sits between it and the hardware to waste resources or add risk. A Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor runs as an app on top of a normal operating system, which suits a laptop lab but not production cloud.

Why it matters to cloud: the hypervisor pools hardware so the provider can carve it up on demand (fast provisioning), keep tenants apart (isolation, so one customer cannot read another's memory), and treat a VM as files. Because a VM is files, it can be snapshotted (a point-in-time copy you can roll back to), cloned from a template (a prepared master image), or live-migrated (moved to another host while still running, for maintenance).

Worked example of overcommitment, meaning handing out more virtual resources than physically exist. A host has 32 cores. Step 1: 16 VMs times 4 virtual CPUs (vCPUs) each equals 64 vCPUs. Step 2: 64 divided by 32 gives a 2:1 overcommit ratio. Step 3: this works because most VMs sit mostly idle, so they rarely all demand CPU at once. Step 4: if they do, VMs wait in line for real cores and slow down.

Common mistake: overcommitting memory as freely as CPU. Idle CPU can be shared easily, but memory that a VM has filled cannot be handed to someone else, so the host starts swapping to disk.

Consequence in a running system: a noisy neighbor, one busy VM on a shared host, makes unrelated VMs sluggish even though their own settings look fine. Choosing dedicated hosts or lower overcommit ratios trades higher cost for predictable performance.

questions.prompt: A video-hosting startup runs a host with 48 physical cores. It places 24 VMs on it, each given 6 vCPUs (virtual CPUs, the processor share a VM believes it owns). Step 1: 24 VMs x 6 vCPUs = 144 vCPUs handed out. Step 2: ??? Step 3: This is safe as long as most VMs stay mostly idle and rarely demand CPU at the same moment. Step 4: If they all get busy at once, VMs queue for real cores and slow down. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: 144 / 24 = 6, so the overcommit ratio is 6:1
144 / 48 = 3, so the overcommit ratio is 3:1
48 / 144 = 0.33, so the overcommit ratio is 1:3
48 / 24 = 2, so the overcommit ratio is 2:1
questions.why: The overcommit ratio compares the virtual CPUs handed out (144) to the physical cores that exist (48), giving 3:1.

questions.prompt: A regional bank is building its own private cloud to host many departments' workloads on shared servers. It wants the virtualization layer to waste as few resources as possible and add as little risk as possible. Which kind of hypervisor (the software that splits a physical server into virtual machines) fits best?
choices: A Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor that runs as an app on a normal operating system
A Type 2 hypervisor, because a full operating system underneath adds isolation
Either type, because both put the same number of layers above the hardware
A Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor that runs directly on the server hardware
questions.why: A Type 1 hypervisor has nothing between it and the hardware, so it avoids the extra overhead and risk of a host operating system, which is why production clouds use it.

questions.prompt: A logistics company must replace a failing power supply in one physical host this afternoon. The VMs on that host run an order-tracking app that customers use all day, so the company wants them to keep running during the repair. Which virtualization capability fits this need?
choices: Take a snapshot of each VM so it can be rolled back after the repair
Live-migrate the VMs to another host while they are still running
Raise the CPU overcommit ratio on the host so VMs finish work faster
Clone each VM from a template onto the same host before the repair
questions.why: Live migration moves a running VM to another host, so the hardware can be serviced without stopping the workload, whereas a snapshot or clone does not keep the VM running elsewhere.

questions.prompt: An administrator at a design agency sees that CPU overcommit at 3:1 works well, so he also hands out three times more VM memory (RAM) than the host physically has. Several VMs then fill their memory at the same time. What is the most likely result?
choices: The host starts swapping memory to disk, and the VMs slow down badly
The host shares the filled memory among VMs the same way it shares idle CPU
Nothing changes, because memory overcommit works exactly like CPU overcommit
The hypervisor live-migrates the busy VMs away, so nothing slows down
questions.why: Memory a VM has filled cannot be handed to another VM the way idle CPU can, so the host falls back to swapping to disk, which slows performance sharply.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why cloud providers depend on virtualization, using the words hypervisor, host, and guest, and name one tradeoff that comes from sharing hardware.
lessons.modelAnswer: Virtualization lets one physical server act as many separate virtual machines. The physical box is the host, each VM is a guest with its own operating system, and the hypervisor is the software that divides the hardware and keeps guests isolated from each other. Cloud providers use Type 1 hypervisors that run directly on the hardware for efficiency and security. This is what makes cloud work: they can spin up a VM in minutes, pack many customers onto shared hardware, and because a VM is just files, snapshot it, clone it from a template, or live-migrate it during maintenance. The tradeoff is sharing. Providers overcommit, for example giving out 64 vCPUs on a 32-core host, betting VMs won't all be busy. When they are, a noisy neighbor can slow everyone. Dedicated hosts avoid that but cost more.
rubricPoints: Defines a hypervisor as the layer that splits a physical host into isolated guest VMs.
Distinguishes Type 1 (bare metal, used in cloud) from Type 2 (hosted on an OS).
Links virtualization to cloud traits like fast provisioning, isolation, and pooling.
Mentions VM-as-files abilities such as snapshots, templates, or live migration.
Names a sharing tradeoff such as overcommitment or noisy neighbors, and a mitigation.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises hypervisors directly, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios like overcommit ratios and dedicated-host choices builds the needed judgment best.

lessons.plain: A cloud virtual network is your own private, fenced-off network inside a cloud provider, built entirely in software. You decide its address range, split it into smaller zones, and write the rules for which traffic may go where. A VPN (virtual private network) is a locked, encrypted tunnel that runs across the public internet to join that cloud network to your office or to one person's laptop. Think of the virtual network as an office building you design floor by floor, and the VPN as a private covered walkway from your old building to the new one. Outsiders can see that the walkway exists, but they cannot see inside it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose your office network and your new cloud network both use addresses that start with 10.0. When a laptop in the office sends data to 10.0.2.15, what problem might the office router have in deciding where to send it?
lessons.teach:
A virtual network is a private, software-defined network that you carve out inside a cloud provider. AWS calls it a VPC and Azure calls it a VNet. You give it an address range written in CIDR notation, such as 10.0.0.0/16. The number after the slash says how many leading bits are fixed, so /16 leaves about 65,000 addresses. You then split that range into subnets, which are smaller blocks such as 10.0.1.0/24 with 256 addresses.

Each subnet follows a route table, a list of rules that says where traffic for each destination goes. A public subnet has a route to an internet gateway, the network's door to the internet. A private subnet has no such route. Its servers reach out through a NAT gateway, which lets them start outbound connections while nothing outside can start one in. Security groups are firewall rules attached to each server, and they allow or deny specific ports.

A VPN is an encrypted tunnel across the public internet. A site-to-site VPN joins a whole office or data centre to the virtual network, usually with IPsec, a standard for encrypting and authenticating packets. A client (point-to-site) VPN connects a single device. VPNs are cheap and quick to set up, but they inherit the internet's variable speed. A dedicated private circuit costs more and gives steadier performance.

Worked example: an office uses 192.168.0.0/16 and needs a database at 10.0.2.15 in a private subnet. A laptop sends a query. The office router knows that 10.0.0.0/16 belongs to the tunnel, so it encrypts the packet and sends it over the internet. The cloud VPN gateway decrypts it, and the subnet delivers it to the database. The database's security group allows port 5432 from 192.168.0.0/16, so the query is accepted. The subnet's route table sends 192.168.0.0/16 back to the VPN gateway, so the reply returns through the tunnel.

Common mistake: using the same range in both places, for example 10.0.0.0/16 in the office and in the cloud. The router cannot tell local addresses from remote ones, so traffic never enters the tunnel. Fixing this later means re-addressing running servers, so plan non-overlapping ranges before you build anything.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's warehouse network uses 172.16.0.0/16. Its cloud virtual network uses 10.40.0.0/16, and an inventory API server sits at 10.40.3.20 in a private subnet. A site-to-site IPsec VPN joins the two. A scanner at 172.16.5.9 calls the API on port 443. Step 1: the warehouse router sees that 10.40.0.0/16 belongs to the tunnel, so it encrypts the packet and sends it across the internet. Step 2: the cloud VPN gateway decrypts it and the subnet delivers it to 10.40.3.20. Step 3: the server's security group allows port 443 from 172.16.0.0/16, so the request is accepted. Step 4: ??? Step 5: the reply travels back through the encrypted tunnel to the scanner. Which statement belongs at Step 4?
choices: The security group also opens port 443 inbound from 0.0.0.0/0 so the reply has a path home.
The private subnet's route table sends 172.16.0.0/16 to the VPN gateway, so the reply enters the tunnel.
The subnet's route table sends 172.16.0.0/16 to the internet gateway, which forwards the reply to the warehouse.
The subnet's route table sends 172.16.0.0/16 to the NAT gateway, which lets the reply out to the warehouse.
questions.why: The reply only goes back through the tunnel if the subnet's route table points the warehouse range at the VPN gateway; a NAT or internet gateway would send it out unencrypted toward the public internet instead.

questions.prompt: A media company runs a transcoding server that must download software updates from the internet, but nothing on the internet should ever be able to start a connection to it. Where should the server be placed?
choices: In a private subnet whose outbound traffic goes through a NAT gateway
In a public subnet behind a client (point-to-site) VPN
In a public subnet with a route to the internet gateway
In a private subnet with a route to the internet gateway
questions.why: A private subnet has no route from the internet gateway, and a NAT gateway lets the server start outbound connections while blocking anything outside from starting one in.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic's office network uses 10.20.0.0/16. Its IT contractor builds a cloud virtual network, also with 10.20.0.0/16, and sets up a site-to-site VPN. Staff report that requests to cloud servers never arrive. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The cloud subnets are /24 blocks, which are too small to accept VPN traffic
The VPN uses IPsec, which cannot carry database traffic
The office router cannot tell local addresses from cloud addresses, so traffic never enters the tunnel
The VPN needs a dedicated private circuit before any traffic can flow
questions.why: When both sides use the same address range, the office router treats the cloud addresses as local, so packets are never sent into the tunnel; fixing it means re-addressing running servers.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm needs to connect its whole head-office network to its cloud virtual network. The link will carry large, time-sensitive data transfers every night, and the firm says steady, predictable performance matters more than cost. Which connection fits best?
choices: A client (point-to-site) VPN installed on the main file server
A NAT gateway in the cloud network's private subnet
A site-to-site IPsec VPN over the public internet
A dedicated private circuit between the office and the cloud provider
questions.why: A VPN is cheap and quick but runs over the internet's variable speed, while a dedicated private circuit costs more and gives the steadier performance the firm asked for.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks how the company's office will reach a database you are putting in the cloud. Explain in your own words how the virtual network should be laid out and how the VPN connects it to the office. Name one limit or tradeoff they should know about.
lessons.modelAnswer: We'll create a virtual network with its own address range, say 10.0.0.0/16, that doesn't overlap the office's 192.168.0.0/16. We split it into subnets. Web servers go in a public subnet whose route table points to an internet gateway. The database goes in a private subnet with no internet route, and it reaches out only through a NAT gateway if it needs updates. A site-to-site VPN using IPsec builds an encrypted tunnel from the office router to the cloud VPN gateway. Routes on both sides send each other's range into that tunnel. The database's security group allows its port only from the office range. The tradeoff is that the VPN rides the public internet, so speed and latency vary. If we need steady performance, a dedicated private circuit costs more. We also can't let address ranges overlap, or routing breaks and we'd have to re-address servers.
rubricPoints: Defines a virtual network as a private, software-defined network with its own address range split into subnets.
Distinguishes public and private subnets by their routes to an internet gateway versus a NAT gateway or no internet route.
Explains that a VPN is an encrypted tunnel over the internet, and separates site-to-site from client VPNs.
Mentions that route tables and security groups both must allow the traffic.
Warns that cloud and on-premises address ranges must not overlap.
Names a tradeoff, such as the VPN's variable internet performance compared with a costlier dedicated circuit.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet hop by hop through route tables, gateways, security groups and a VPN tunnel is exactly what the planned virtual network path tracer would let the learner practise.

lessons.plain: Containerization means packaging an application together with everything it needs to run, such as its libraries, settings and runtime, into one sealed, portable unit called a container. Think of a shipping container: whatever is inside, every ship, truck and crane handles the box the same way. A container behaves the same on a laptop, a test server or a cloud provider. Containers share the host computer's operating system core instead of each carrying a full operating system. That makes them small and quick to start. In the cloud, this lets teams move apps between environments easily, pack many apps onto fewer machines, and add copies quickly when demand grows.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer says 'it works on my laptop' but the same app crashes on the cloud server because a library version is different. What would you bundle with the app so it behaves the same everywhere?
lessons.teach:
A container is an isolated, running copy of an application that carries its own code, libraries and configuration but shares the host's kernel. The kernel is the core of the operating system that manages memory, CPU and devices. A container image is the read-only template a container starts from, like a recipe. A container runtime is the software on a host that starts and stops containers from images. A registry is a storage service, often a managed cloud service, that holds images so any host can download them.

This works because the image fixes every dependency at build time. Every host that runs it gets identical contents. Containers skip booting a full guest operating system, so they start in seconds and use little memory. That is the contrast with a virtual machine, which carries its own whole operating system. The result is portability, density (more apps per server) and fast scaling, which fits microservices. A microservice is a small, independently deployable piece of a larger application.

Worked example: a team packages its order API. Step 1, they build an image containing the API code and its exact library versions. Step 2, they push the image to a registry. Step 3, a test server pulls the image and runs it, and it behaves exactly as it did on the laptop. Step 4, at a sales peak, the cloud host runs three containers from the same image in seconds, and traffic spreads across them.

Common mistake: storing important data inside the container. Containers are ephemeral, meaning they can be replaced at any time, and anything written inside is lost when that happens. In a running system, a restarted database container could wipe customer records. Persistent data belongs in attached storage volumes or a managed database. Also, shared-kernel isolation is weaker than a virtual machine's, so untrusted workloads may need stronger separation.

Managing many containers across many hosts is the job of orchestration, which is a separate topic.

questions.prompt: A regional bus company moves its ticket-scanning service into containers. Riders' scanned tickets must be kept for 90 days for audits. The team works through it like this. Step 1: they build an image with the scanning code and its pinned library versions. Step 2: the container runtime on two cloud hosts starts four containers from that image. Step 3: (missing) they decide where each container writes the scanned ticket records. Step 4: a host is patched overnight and all its containers are replaced by new ones, and every record from the previous day is still available the next morning. Which choice for Step 3 makes Step 4 come true?
choices: Write the records to the container's own internal filesystem, since each container has its own isolated copy of the application
Write the records to an attached storage volume or a managed database that lives outside the containers
Run eight containers instead of four so that at least one copy of each record survives a replacement
Add the records to the image each night so every new container starts with them already inside
questions.why: Containers are ephemeral and lose anything written inside them when replaced, so data that must last has to go to storage outside the container, such as an attached volume or a managed database.

questions.prompt: An engineer compares a container with a virtual machine (VM). Which statement correctly describes the key difference?
choices: A container shares the host's kernel, while a VM carries its own whole operating system
A container can only run on a laptop, while a VM can only run in the cloud
A container carries its own full operating system, while a VM shares the host's kernel
A container is a read-only template, while a VM is a running copy of an application
questions.why: Containers bundle their code, libraries and configuration but share the host's kernel, whereas a VM includes an entire guest operating system of its own.

questions.prompt: An online florist has split its website into small, independently deployable services (microservices). On Valentine's Day its traffic jumps tenfold within minutes, and it needs extra copies of the checkout service running almost immediately. Why are containers a good fit for this?
choices: Containers give stronger isolation than VMs, so more copies can safely share a host
Containers store customer data inside themselves, so new copies arrive already holding orders
Containers each boot their own guest operating system, which makes every copy fully independent
Containers skip booting a full guest operating system, so new copies start in seconds from the same image
questions.why: Because a container shares the host's kernel instead of booting a whole operating system, many identical copies can start from one image in seconds, which suits fast scaling.

questions.prompt: A coding-challenge website plans to run programs uploaded by anonymous members of the public, packing many of these programs as containers onto the same cloud hosts. What is the main concern with this plan?
choices: The containers will start too slowly, because each one must boot its own full operating system
The containers will behave differently on each host, because images change their libraries at run time
The containers cannot be downloaded from a registry, so each host would need its own copy built locally
The containers share the host's kernel, so isolation is weaker than a VM's and untrusted code may need stronger separation
questions.why: Shared-kernel isolation is weaker than a virtual machine's, so untrusted workloads like code from anonymous users may need stronger separation such as running in VMs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why your team might containerize an application before moving it to the cloud, and name at least one limit or tradeoff of containers.
lessons.modelAnswer: A container bundles our app with its exact libraries and settings into an image. Any host with a container runtime can run that image the same way, so 'works on my laptop' becomes 'works everywhere.' We store images in a registry, and test, staging and cloud hosts all pull the same one. Containers share the host's kernel instead of booting a full operating system, so they are small and start in seconds. We can pack more of them per server and add copies quickly when traffic spikes, which suits microservices. The tradeoffs: containers are ephemeral, so any data written inside one disappears when it is replaced. Databases and uploads need external volumes or managed storage. Because they share a kernel, their isolation is weaker than a virtual machine's. And once we run many of them, we will need orchestration to manage them.
rubricPoints: Defines a container as an app packaged with its dependencies, built from an image.
Explains that sharing the host kernel makes containers lightweight and fast to start compared with full virtual machines.
Names cloud benefits such as portability across environments, density, and rapid scaling.
Mentions images stored in a registry and pulled by any host.
Identifies a limit such as ephemeral storage or weaker isolation than virtual machines.

suggested.rationale: No current mission builds or runs containers, so reasoning through exam-style workload scenarios that ask whether to containerize, and how to handle state, best builds the recommendation skill this unit targets.

lessons.plain: Container orchestration is software that runs and looks after many containers across a group of machines for you. A container is a small, self-contained package of an application and everything it needs to run. Once you have dozens or hundreds of containers, starting, moving and fixing them by hand stops being realistic. An orchestrator is like a restaurant floor manager. You tell it 'keep three tables staffed at all times', and it assigns waiters, replaces anyone who goes home sick, and adds staff when the room fills up. You say what you want, and it keeps making that true.
lessons.guessPrompt: You run three copies of a web app in containers, one on each of three servers. At 3 a.m. one server loses power. What would you want to happen automatically, and what would a person have to do if nothing handled it?
lessons.teach:
Container orchestration is software that automatically places, runs, connects, scales and repairs containers across a group of machines. A container is an application packaged with everything it needs, and it shares the host's operating system kernel. A cluster is the group of machines, called nodes, that the orchestrator manages. Kubernetes is the most widely used orchestrator, and cloud providers offer managed versions where they run its control layer for you.

It works through desired state. You declare what you want, usually in a configuration file, for example 'three replicas of the web app, each requesting 0.5 CPU and 512 MB of memory'. A replica is one running copy. A control loop keeps comparing the desired state with the actual state and acts to close any gap. That one idea gives you several features. Scheduling means choosing a node with enough free capacity. Self-healing means replacing failed copies. Scaling means changing the replica count, either by hand or from a metric such as CPU. Rolling updates replace old versions a few at a time so the service stays up, and roll back if health checks fail. Service discovery gives the app a stable name and address that spreads traffic across whichever replicas exist right now.

Worked example. The desired state is 3 replicas, and 3 are running, one each on nodes A, B and C. Node C loses power. Step 1: the orchestrator notices C has stopped reporting, so the actual count is 2. Step 2: it sees a gap of 1. Step 3: the scheduler checks A and B for free CPU and memory and starts a new replica on A. Step 4: the new replica passes its health check and starts receiving traffic. Actual matches desired again, and nobody was woken up.

A common mistake is saving important data inside the container's own filesystem. Orchestrators treat containers as disposable, so a replacement starts fresh and that data is lost. Keep state in persistent volumes, which is storage attached from outside the container, or in a managed database. A second mistake is leaving out resource requests. The scheduler then packs too much onto nodes, and under load containers are killed for running out of memory, which leads to restart loops.

questions.prompt: A city library runs its book-search app on a container orchestrator. The desired state is 2 replicas, each requesting 0.25 CPU and 256 MB of memory, plus a scaling rule: if average CPU stays above 70%, raise the replica count to 4. On exam-results morning, student traffic spikes. Step 1: the orchestrator reads the CPU metric and sees it holding at 90%, above the 70% threshold. Step 2: following the rule, it changes the desired count from 2 to 4, so the control loop now sees a gap of 2 replicas. Step 3: ______. Step 4: the two new replicas pass their health checks, and the app's stable service name begins spreading search traffic across all 4 replicas. What is the missing Step 3?
choices: The orchestrator copies the files saved inside the existing replicas' own filesystems into the new replicas, so they share the same stored data.
The orchestrator pages an administrator, who logs in to two nodes and starts the new copies by hand, because scaling cannot happen without a person.
The orchestrator removes the old version of the app and starts the newer version two copies at a time, because extra replicas always mean an update.
The scheduler looks for nodes with enough free CPU and memory to fit each new replica's 0.25 CPU and 256 MB request, and starts the two new replicas there.
questions.why: Closing a gap in the replica count requires scheduling, which means placing each new copy on a node that has enough free capacity for its declared resource requests.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a shipping company writes a configuration file stating that the tracking service should always have 5 running copies. Later, 1 copy crashes and the orchestrator starts a replacement without anyone asking it to. Which idea explains this behaviour?
choices: Rolling updates: the orchestrator replaces copies a few at a time whenever a new version is published.
Persistent volumes: storage attached from outside the container restarts the crashed copy from saved data.
Desired state: a control loop keeps comparing what was declared with what is actually running, and acts to close any gap.
Service discovery: the service's stable name automatically creates new copies whenever traffic reaches it.
questions.why: Self-healing comes from the desired-state control loop: 4 running against 5 declared is a gap of 1, so the orchestrator starts a replacement.

questions.prompt: A photo-printing startup runs its upload app as 3 replicas on a managed Kubernetes cluster. Customers' uploaded photos are saved inside each container's own filesystem. After a node fails and the orchestrator replaces a replica, customers report that some of their photos have vanished. What change best fixes this?
choices: Turn on rolling updates so that replicas are replaced only a few at a time.
Store the photos in a persistent volume attached from outside the container, or in a managed database, instead of in the container's filesystem.
Add a CPU-based scaling rule so the app scales out before a node can fail.
Increase the replica count from 3 to 6 so that more copies of each photo exist.
questions.why: The orchestrator treats containers as disposable, and a replacement starts with a fresh filesystem, so data must live in storage outside the container to survive.

questions.prompt: A payroll team deploys 8 replicas of a reporting service but leaves out the CPU and memory requests in the configuration. Everything looks fine at first. At month-end, when load is heavy, what is the most likely result?
choices: The scheduler refuses to start any replicas until requests are added, so the service never comes up.
The orchestrator rolls the service back to an earlier version, because missing requests count as a failed health check.
The scheduler packs too many replicas onto some nodes, and under load containers are killed for running out of memory, causing restart loops.
Service discovery stops working, because the stable name and address depend on the resource requests.
questions.why: Without resource requests, the scheduler cannot tell how much capacity each replica needs, so it overloads nodes, and heavy load then leads to out-of-memory kills and restart loops.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how a container orchestrator keeps an application running when a node fails, and name one limit or tradeoff they need to design around.
lessons.modelAnswer: With an orchestrator such as Kubernetes, we don't start containers by hand. We declare a desired state, for example three replicas of our API with set CPU and memory requests. A control loop keeps comparing that against what is actually running. If a node dies, the running count drops below three. The scheduler then finds another node with enough spare capacity, starts a replacement, waits for its health check, and the service's stable address begins routing traffic to it. The same loop handles scaling and rolling updates. The tradeoff is that containers are treated as disposable. Anything written inside a container is lost when it's replaced, so state must live in persistent volumes or a database. Self-healing also only works if the cluster has spare capacity and our resource requests are realistic. Otherwise there's nowhere to reschedule, and pods crash for lack of memory.
rubricPoints: Defines orchestration as automated placement, scaling and repair of containers across a cluster of nodes.
Explains desired state and the control loop that keeps reconciling it with the actual state.
Traces node failure: the loss is detected, the scheduler picks a node with capacity, and a health check is passed before traffic arrives.
Mentions related features such as scaling, rolling updates or service discovery.
Names a limit: containers are disposable so state needs external storage, or spare capacity and accurate resource requests are required.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine runs an orchestrator end to end, so reasoning through exam-style workload scenarios about desired state, self-healing, scaling and stateful data builds this skill best.

lessons.plain: A database is the organised store where an application keeps the facts it must remember: customers, orders, sensor readings. In the cloud you usually rent a managed database, where the provider handles the hardware, patching and backups while you handle the data and how your app uses it. There are two broad families. Relational databases are like strict spreadsheets with fixed columns that link to each other. Non-relational databases are more like labelled folders, where each item can have its own shape. Picking the right family, and deciding how copies of the data are kept, shapes how fast, reliable and costly the app is.
lessons.guessPrompt: An online shop's single database is overloaded. About 90% of requests are people browsing products and only 10% are placing orders. Without rewriting the app, what kind of extra database copy might take pressure off, and what could go wrong with it?
lessons.teach:
A relational database stores data in tables with a fixed schema (a declared set of columns and types) and is queried with SQL, a standard query language. It supports transactions, groups of changes that all succeed or all fail, which suits orders, payments and inventory. A non-relational (NoSQL) database stores data as key-value pairs, documents or similar flexible shapes. It trades some strictness for easy horizontal scaling (adding more machines) instead of vertical scaling (buying a bigger machine), which suits huge volumes of simple lookups such as sessions or telemetry.

A managed database service (often called DBaaS, database as a service) runs the engine for you: the provider patches it, takes automated backups and can fail over to a standby copy. You still own the schema, the queries and the access rules.

Most cloud databases use replication, copying data from a primary (the only copy that accepts writes) to replicas. A synchronous replica confirms each write before the app is told it succeeded, which is safe but slower. An asynchronous read replica receives changes slightly later, so it can serve read traffic cheaply. The delay is called replication lag.

Worked example: a fleet app writes a truck's position to the primary at 09:00:00. Replication to the read replica is asynchronous and currently lagging 40 seconds. A dispatcher's map reads from the replica at 09:00:10. The replica has not yet received the 09:00:00 row, so the map shows where the truck was earlier. At 09:00:40 the row arrives and the map catches up.

A common mistake is treating a replica as a backup. Replication copies mistakes too: if someone deletes a table on the primary, the replica deletes it seconds later. Only point-in-time backups let you restore. A second mistake is sending every read to replicas, including reads that must see a write the user just made. In a running system that shows users stale data; such reads belong on the primary, and lag should be monitored with an alarm.

questions.prompt: A recipe website saves a user's new comment to the primary database at 14:30:00. Replication to the read replica is asynchronous, and lag is currently 25 seconds. The comments page reads only from the replica. Step 1: the write is accepted by the primary at 14:30:00. Step 2: with 25 seconds of lag, the comment should reach the replica at about 14:30:25. Step 3: another visitor loads the comments page at 14:30:12, and the page reads from the replica. Step 4: ??? Step 5: at 14:30:25 the replica receives the comment, and page loads after that show it. What belongs in Step 4?
choices: The page shows the new comment, because the primary has already confirmed the write to the app
The page returns an error, because a replica refuses reads while a change is still on its way
The page shows the comments without the new one, because the replica has not received that write yet
The replica fetches the missing comment from the primary on demand, so the page is fully current
questions.why: At 14:30:12 the write is still inside the 25-second lag window, so the asynchronous replica serves its older data without the new comment.

questions.prompt: A utility company collects a reading from millions of smart meters every minute. Each reading is a simple meter-ID and value pair that is later looked up by meter ID, and the volume keeps growing. Which database approach fits best?
choices: A single relational table on the largest available machine, because transactions are needed for every reading
A non-relational (NoSQL) key-value store, because it handles huge volumes of simple lookups and scales horizontally by adding machines
An asynchronous read replica only, because replicas can accept the writes cheaply
A relational database scaled vertically, because a fixed schema is required for any numeric data
questions.why: High-volume, simple key-based telemetry suits NoSQL, which trades some strictness for easy horizontal scaling.

questions.prompt: At a clinic booking service, an engineer accidentally runs a command that deletes the appointments table on the primary database at 11:05. The database has two read replicas and point-in-time backups enabled. What is the correct way to get the data back?
choices: Promote one of the read replicas, since replicas keep a separate safe copy of the data
Switch the app to read from the synchronous replica, which never copies deletions
Wait for replication lag to finish, after which the replicas resend the table to the primary
Restore from a point-in-time backup taken before 11:05
questions.why: Replication copies the deletion to replicas within seconds, so only a point-in-time backup from before the mistake can restore the table.

questions.prompt: A startup moves its customer database to a managed database service (DBaaS). Which task does the startup still own after the move?
choices: Applying security patches to the database engine
Failing over to a standby copy when the primary machine breaks
Deciding who is allowed to access which data and designing the tables and queries
Taking the routine automated backups
questions.why: A managed service handles patching, automated backups and failover, but the customer still owns the schema, the queries and the access rules.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would add a read replica to a cloud database, and name the tradeoff it brings and one thing it does not protect you from.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd add a read replica when the database is busy mostly with reads, like browsing or dashboards, and the primary is struggling. The primary keeps handling all writes, while the replica, which gets copies of changes asynchronously, absorbs the read load. That's usually cheaper and simpler than a much bigger single server. The tradeoff is replication lag: the replica can be seconds or more behind, so anything that must reflect a write the user just made, such as showing an order they just placed, should still read from the primary, and we should alarm on lag. A replica also isn't a backup. If someone deletes data or corrupts a table on the primary, that change replicates too, so we still need automated point-in-time backups from the managed service to recover.
rubricPoints: The primary takes all writes and read replicas serve read traffic.
Asynchronous replication causes lag, so replicas can return stale data.
Reads that must see a just-made write should go to the primary.
A replica is not a backup because deletions and corruption replicate too.
Lag should be monitored so stale reads are noticed.

suggested.rationale: The replica-lag incident makes the learner diagnose stale reads from an asynchronous replica, which is the core database tradeoff in this lesson.

lessons.plain: Optimizing cloud resources means paying for what a workload actually needs, while still giving it enough power to run well. In the cloud you rent computing by the hour or second, so a server that is mostly idle wastes money. A server that is too small makes users wait. Think of renting a moving truck. Too big and you pay for empty space. Too small and you need extra trips. Optimizing means measuring how much of each resource the workload really uses, then adjusting size, count, schedule or storage type until cost and speed are both acceptable.
lessons.guessPrompt: A test server sits at about 5% CPU all week and nobody uses it at night or on weekends. Name two changes you could make to cut its cost without hurting the people who use it.
lessons.teach:
Optimizing cloud resources means matching the capacity you pay for to the capacity a workload actually uses. The goal is good performance without paying for idle hardware. A few moves cover most cases.

Right-sizing means changing an instance (a rented virtual machine with a fixed amount of CPU and memory) to a smaller or larger size. You base the choice on utilization, the share of that capacity actually in use. Vertical scaling makes one machine bigger. Horizontal scaling adds or removes identical copies behind a load balancer, a service that spreads incoming requests across those copies. Autoscaling does horizontal scaling automatically when a metric such as CPU crosses a threshold you set. Scheduling means switching off non-production resources when nobody needs them. Storage tiering means moving rarely read data to cheaper, slower storage classes.

These moves work because cloud billing is usage-based. Capacity you provision but never use is pure cost. Capacity you lack shows up as slow responses or errors.

Here is a worked example. A reporting server has 16 virtual CPUs and 64 GB of memory. Two weeks of monitoring show average CPU at 12%, peak CPU at 30% and memory at 20%.
Step 1: real peak demand is 30% of 16, about 5 CPUs. Memory use is about 13 GB.
Step 2: leave headroom (spare capacity for surprises) by aiming for peaks near 60 to 70%.
Step 3: an 8-CPU, 32 GB size would put peak CPU near 60% and memory near 40%.
Step 4: resize, then keep watching response times for a week. If the price tracks size, the cost roughly halves.

A common mistake is sizing to the average instead of the peak. Another is shrinking a spiky workload that should autoscale instead. In a running system, a machine sized to its average runs out of CPU at the daily peak. Requests queue, latency climbs and users see timeouts.

The opposite mistake is autoscaling with no maximum. A traffic spike or a bug can then add copies without limit and inflate the bill. Good optimization is a loop: measure, adjust, then measure again.

questions.prompt:
A logistics company runs a route-planning API on an instance with 12 virtual CPUs and 48 GB of memory. Three weeks of monitoring show average CPU at 8%, peak CPU at 20% and memory use at 20%.
Step 1: real peak demand is 20% of 12, about 2.4 CPUs. Memory use is about 9.6 GB.
Step 2: leave headroom by aiming for peaks near 60 to 70% of the new size.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: resize, then keep watching response times for a week before deciding whether to adjust again.
Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Keep 12 vCPUs and 48 GB, because peak CPU at 20% shows the API is already busy enough at its peak.
Pick 8 vCPUs and 32 GB, which puts peak CPU near 30%, so the API has plenty of spare room at all times.
Pick 4 vCPUs and 16 GB, which puts peak CPU near 60% and memory near 60%, inside the target headroom.
Pick 2 vCPUs and 8 GB, because the average CPU of 8% means only about 1 CPU is needed most of the time.
questions.why: About 2.4 CPUs out of 4 and about 9.6 GB out of 16 GB both land near 60%, which meets peak demand with headroom without paying for idle capacity.

questions.prompt: A design agency keeps a test environment of six virtual machines. The machines run 24 hours a day, but the testers only use them from 9:00 to 18:00 on weekdays. Which optimization move fits this situation best?
choices: Scheduling: switch the test machines off outside working hours and on weekends.
Storage tiering: move the test machines' data to a cheaper, slower storage class.
Vertical scaling: give each test machine more CPU and memory so tests finish faster.
Autoscaling with no maximum, so the environment can grow whenever testers need it.
questions.why: Scheduling switches off non-production resources when nobody needs them, so the agency stops paying for the hours the machines sit idle.

questions.prompt: An online bakery shrank its order server so that it runs at about 70% CPU on an average day. Every evening around 19:00, when orders peak, customers report slow pages and checkout timeouts. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The load balancer is spreading requests across too many identical copies of the server.
The server was sized to its average load, so it runs out of CPU at the daily peak.
The server was moved to a cheaper storage class, so order data is read too slowly.
An autoscaling group has no maximum, so it keeps adding copies during the evening.
questions.why: Sizing to the average instead of the peak leaves no capacity for the evening spike, so requests queue, latency climbs and users see timeouts.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticket website gets steady light traffic most of the month, then a huge burst of visitors whenever a popular show goes on sale. The team wants extra web servers to appear during a burst and disappear afterwards, without anyone acting by hand, and does not want the bill to grow without limit if a bug causes runaway traffic. Which setup matches this goal?
choices: Vertical scaling: resize the single web server to a larger size every time a show goes on sale.
Right-sizing the web server to the average monthly CPU so the team stops paying for idle capacity.
Autoscaling of identical servers behind a load balancer, triggered by a CPU threshold, with no maximum.
Autoscaling of identical servers behind a load balancer, triggered by a CPU threshold, with a set maximum.
questions.why: Autoscaling adds and removes identical copies automatically when a metric crosses a threshold, and a maximum stops a spike or bug from inflating the bill.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether to right-size, autoscale or schedule a given cloud workload. Name one tradeoff or risk of cutting capacity.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I'd collect a couple of weeks of utilization data for CPU and memory, looking at both averages and peaks. If the load is steady and the machine is clearly oversized, I'd right-size it to a smaller instance, leaving headroom so the peak lands around 60 to 70%. If the load is spiky, with quiet hours and sudden surges, I'd use horizontal autoscaling behind a load balancer. I'd set a minimum so we're never empty and a maximum so costs can't run away. If it's a dev or test system nobody uses at night, I'd schedule it off outside working hours. The tradeoff is that every cut in capacity reduces headroom. If I size to the average or trim too far, the next peak causes queuing, slow responses and timeouts. So I'd change one thing at a time and keep monitoring afterward.
rubricPoints: Decisions are based on measured utilization, including peaks and not just averages.
Right-sizing suits steady loads on oversized instances, and headroom is left for spikes.
Autoscaling suits variable loads and needs sensible minimum and maximum limits.
Scheduling idle non-production resources off saves cost with little performance risk.
Cutting capacity too far causes latency or errors at peak, so changes must be verified with ongoing monitoring.

suggested.rationale: The unit's core skill is choosing the right optimization move for a described workload, which is best practiced by reasoning through exam-style scenarios that contrast steady, spiky and idle workloads.

lessons.plain: Cloud billing works like a utility meter rather than a one-time purchase. Instead of buying servers up front, you are charged for what you use: compute hours, gigabytes stored, data sent out, and requests made. Billing management means watching that meter, deciding which pricing deal fits each workload, and making sure every charge can be traced to the team or project that caused it. Think of a household electricity bill. Leaving lights on in empty rooms costs money, and a fixed-rate plan only saves you money if you really use that much power.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server only needs to run during office hours, about 8 hours a day on weekdays. Would you rather pay a lower hourly rate by committing to run it all year, or pay a higher hourly rate only for the hours it actually runs? Why?
lessons.teach:
Billing management is the practice of tracking, predicting, and controlling what a cloud provider charges you. The main idea is usage-based pricing: each resource has a meter, and the bill is the rate multiplied by the amount used.

The pricing models are as follows. On-demand means pay-as-you-go at the full rate with no commitment. Reserved or committed-use pricing means you promise to pay for a resource for one or three years in exchange for a discount, and you pay whether you use it or not. Spot or preemptible pricing means you use the provider's spare capacity very cheaply, but it can be taken back at short notice, so it suits interruptible jobs like batch processing. Licensing is also a cost: BYOL (bring your own license) lets you reuse software licenses you already own instead of paying for licenses bundled into the hourly price.

To know who is spending, you tag resources, which means attaching labels such as project or cost center. Showback reports each team's spending to them without billing them. Chargeback actually bills that cost to each team's budget. Budgets and alerts warn you when spending crosses a set limit.

Here is a worked example in fictional credits. A virtual machine costs 0.10 per hour on demand. Running it all month (about 730 hours) costs 73. A one-year reservation gives a 40% discount, so the cost is 43.80 per month, paid regardless of use. Now suppose the workload only runs about 176 hours a month, which is office hours on weekdays. On demand, that costs 17.60. The reservation would waste money here. Reserve steady 24/7 workloads, and leave part-time ones on demand.

A common mistake is pricing only compute. Data egress, meaning data leaving the provider's network, is often charged while data coming in is free. Storage of forgotten snapshots and idle resources also keeps billing. In a running system, these hidden meters cause surprise bills, and untagged resources make it impossible to say which team should fix them.

questions.prompt: A design studio runs a file-conversion server priced at 0.50 credits per hour on demand. A one-year reservation would give a 45% discount. The server only runs about 300 hours a month, and a full month is about 730 hours. Step 1: the on-demand monthly cost is 0.50 × 300 = 150 credits. Step 2: work out the reserved monthly cost. Step 3: compare the two figures and pick the cheaper model. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: 0.50 × 0.55 × 730 = 200.75 credits, because a reservation is paid for every hour of the month, used or not
0.50 × 730 = 365 credits, because a reservation always charges the full on-demand rate for the whole month
0.50 × 0.55 × 300 = 82.50 credits, because the discounted rate applies only to the hours the server actually runs
0.50 × 0.45 × 730 = 164.25 credits, because 45% is the share of the full rate you still pay
questions.why: A 45% discount leaves 55% of the 0.50 rate, and a reservation is paid for every hour of the month whether the server runs or not, so the cost is 0.50 × 0.55 × 730 = 200.75 credits. That is more than 150, so this part-time server should stay on demand.

questions.prompt: A research lab renders animation frames overnight. If a job is interrupted, it simply restarts that frame later, and the lab wants the lowest possible compute price. Which pricing model fits best?
choices: A three-year reservation, because long commitments always give the lowest total bill
Bring your own license (BYOL), because it removes the hourly charge for compute
Spot or preemptible pricing, because the jobs can tolerate capacity being taken back at short notice
On-demand pricing, because only on-demand machines can run batch jobs
questions.why: Spot capacity is very cheap but can be reclaimed at short notice, which suits interruptible batch work like restartable rendering.

questions.prompt: A retailer moved its reporting app to the cloud. The virtual machine costs matched the estimate exactly, yet the monthly bill was much higher. The app sends large report files to thousands of customers over the internet every day. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Data coming into the provider's network from customers is charged at a high rate
The machines should have been tagged, because untagged resources cost more per hour
The machines are on spot pricing, which charges extra whenever capacity is reclaimed
Data egress charges for the report files leaving the provider's network
questions.why: Data leaving the provider's network (egress) is often charged while incoming data is free, so a cost estimate that covers only compute misses it.

questions.prompt: A company's finance team wants each department to see a monthly report of its own cloud spending, without moving any money out of department budgets yet. Which practice is this, and what must be in place for it to work?
choices: Budgets and alerts, which need every resource to run on demand
Chargeback, which needs spot pricing so costs can be split by team
Showback, which needs resources tagged with labels such as department or cost center
Chargeback, which needs a reservation for each department's resources
questions.why: Showback reports spending to each team without billing them, and tags such as cost center are what let the spending be attributed to the right department.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between on-demand, reserved, and spot pricing for a workload, and name one cost that people often forget to include.
lessons.modelAnswer: Cloud costs are usage-based: every resource has a meter, and the bill is rate times usage. I pick the pricing model based on how the workload behaves. If it runs steadily around the clock for a year or more, a reservation or committed-use deal saves money, because the discount beats on-demand. The tradeoff is that you pay even when the resource is idle, so reserving a part-time workload wastes money. If the usage is unpredictable or part-time, on-demand is safer. If the job can be interrupted and restarted, like batch processing, spot capacity is cheapest, but it can be reclaimed with little warning. The costs people forget are data egress charges for data leaving the provider, plus idle resources and old snapshots. I'd also tag everything so we can show back or charge back costs to the right team, and I'd set budget alerts to catch surprises early.
rubricPoints: Cloud billing is usage-based: rate multiplied by amount used.
Reserved or committed pricing gives a discount but is paid whether used or not, so it fits steady workloads.
Spot pricing is cheapest but interruptible, so it suits restartable jobs.
Hidden costs such as data egress, idle resources, or stored snapshots must be included.
Tagging enables showback or chargeback so costs can be traced to teams.
Budgets and alerts catch overspending early.

suggested.rationale: A cost model in fictional credits would let the learner compare on-demand, reserved, and spot pricing and spot egress and idle charges by actually calculating bills.

lessons.plain: Before you move a workload to the cloud, you study what it really needs. A workload is an application plus the servers, data and connections it relies on. You check how much computing power, memory, storage and network it actually uses. You note which other systems it talks to, what software and licences it depends on, and what rules it must follow. It is like measuring a household before a move: count the furniture, measure the big pieces, note what must travel together, and check the new doorways. Skip this and the sofa gets stuck on moving day.
lessons.guessPrompt: An old server has 16 processor cores and 64 GB of memory, but it rarely uses more than a third of either. If you rent a cloud server for this application, should it have the same 16 cores and 64 GB? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Requirements analysis means collecting facts about a workload before you choose any cloud resources. It has four parts.

The first is a performance baseline: measured utilization over time. Utilization is the share of a resource actually in use. You track CPU (processing power), memory, storage capacity, IOPS (input/output operations per second, meaning how many disk reads and writes happen each second) and network throughput. You record both the average and the peak, which is the highest point.

The second is dependency mapping: listing every system the workload talks to, such as databases, licence servers and authentication services.

The third is compatibility: confirming that the operating system, software versions and licence terms are allowed in the target cloud.

The fourth is non-functional requirements. These cover availability targets in the SLA (service level agreement, a promised uptime level) and compliance rules such as data sovereignty, which means data must stay in a certain country.

Worked example. A reporting server has 16 vCPU (virtual CPUs) and 64 GB of memory. You monitor it for a full month. CPU averages 15% and peaks at 40% during month-end reports. Peak CPU is 40% of 16, which is 6.4 vCPU. Adding 25% headroom, meaning spare capacity for growth and spikes, gives 8 vCPU. Memory peaks at 24 GB, and 24 plus 25% is 30 GB, so you choose a 32 GB size. Dependency mapping shows the server queries a database on another host many times per report. That database should move in the same wave, or every query will cross a slow link between the old site and the cloud. The result is right-sizing: 8 vCPU and 32 GB instead of a copy of the old 16 and 64.

The common mistake is measuring too short a window or using only averages. A one-week sample here would have missed the month-end peak. The server would be sized at about 3 vCPU and would slow badly, or time out, on the first month-end after migration. Copying the old specification makes the opposite error and wastes money every hour the oversized server runs.

questions.prompt: A logistics company plans to move an order-processing server that has 12 vCPU and 48 GB of memory. The team monitors it for a full quarter. CPU peaks at 50%, so peak need is 0.5 × 12 = 6 vCPU, and adding 25% headroom gives 7.5, so they pick 8 vCPU. Memory averages 10 GB and peaks at 16 GB. The available memory sizes are 16 GB, 24 GB and 32 GB. Missing step: what memory size should they choose, and why?
choices: Add 25% headroom to the 10 GB average to get 12.5 GB, then choose 16 GB
Add 25% headroom to the 16 GB peak to get 20 GB, then choose the 24 GB size
Choose 16 GB, because the measured peak of 16 GB fits that size exactly
Choose 48 GB to match the old server, so performance cannot get any worse
questions.why: Right-sizing applies headroom to the measured peak (16 × 1.25 = 20 GB) and then rounds up to the next available size, which is 24 GB.

questions.prompt: During a month of monitoring, a storage server's disk handles at most 2,500 reads and 1,500 writes in a single second, at its busiest moment. Which baseline figure have you just captured?
choices: Average IOPS of 2,000
Peak storage capacity of 4,000
Peak IOPS of 4,000
Peak network throughput of 4,000
questions.why: IOPS counts disk reads plus writes per second, and the busiest second is the peak, so 2,500 + 1,500 gives a peak of 4,000 IOPS.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic chain in Canada is moving its patient-records system to the cloud. A provincial rule says patient data must be stored only inside Canada. Which part of requirements analysis does this rule belong to?
choices: Non-functional requirements, as a data sovereignty compliance rule
Performance baseline, because it affects storage capacity
Dependency mapping, because it lists systems the workload talks to
Compatibility, because it limits which operating systems are allowed
questions.why: Data sovereignty, meaning data must stay in a certain country, is a compliance rule, and compliance rules are part of non-functional requirements.

questions.prompt: A team monitors a payroll application for five days in the middle of the month and sizes the cloud server from the average CPU they saw. Payroll is calculated on the last day of each month. What is the most likely result after migration?
choices: Nothing, because averages already include any short busy periods
The server will be oversized and waste money every hour it runs
The licence terms will be broken in the target cloud
The server will slow badly or time out on the first month-end payroll run
questions.why: A short mid-month window and averages miss the month-end peak, so the server is undersized and struggles when the real peak arrives.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we baseline a server before migrating it instead of just copying its hardware specification, and name one limit or tradeoff of the baseline approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Copying the old hardware specification tells us what the server has, not what it uses. A baseline measures real CPU, memory, disk IOPS and network use over time, both average and peak. Then we size to the peak plus some headroom. That usually lets us right-size to something smaller and cheaper, and it still covers the busiest moments. We also map dependencies, so tightly linked systems such as an app and its database move together. We check compatibility and compliance, such as licences and where data is allowed to live. The limit is that a baseline only reflects the window we measured. If we sample a quiet week, we miss month-end or seasonal peaks and undersize the server. A longer window costs time before the migration can start. Headroom is a tradeoff too: more headroom is safer but costs more.
rubricPoints: A baseline measures actual utilization, not installed hardware.
Sizing uses peak values plus headroom, not averages alone.
Dependency mapping finds systems that must migrate together.
Compatibility, licensing and compliance rules such as data sovereignty are checked too.
The measurement window must include real peaks, or the server ends up undersized.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine covers pre-migration sizing directly, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios with given utilization numbers and dependencies builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Infrastructure as code (IaC) means describing your servers, networks, storage and permissions in text files instead of building them by hand in a web console. A tool reads those files and creates or changes the real cloud resources to match. Think of it like a recipe card versus cooking from memory: anyone can follow the card and get the same dish every time, you can see exactly what changed between versions, and if the kitchen burns down you can cook it again. Because the files live alongside application code, teams can review, test and repeat their infrastructure builds instead of hoping someone remembers which buttons they clicked.
lessons.guessPrompt: A teammate fixed a production firewall rule by clicking in the cloud console, but the team builds everything from IaC files. The next time the IaC tool runs, what do you think happens to that hand-made fix, and why?
lessons.teach:
Infrastructure as code (IaC) is the practice of defining cloud resources in machine-readable files, called templates, and letting a tool build them. There are two styles. A declarative template states the desired end result ("two virtual machines, one private network") and the tool works out the steps. An imperative script lists the steps themselves ("create a network, then create a machine"). Most cloud IaC is declarative; configuration management tools, which install software and settings inside machines, can be either.

It works because of idempotency: applying the same template many times gives the same result, creating only what is missing. Declarative tools keep a state record of what they built, compare it with the template and with the real cloud, then plan only the differences. Templates are stored in version control (a system that tracks every change, who made it and why), so infrastructure changes get reviewed like code and can be rolled back.

Worked example: a template declares one virtual network and two web servers. First run: the tool sees nothing exists, plans three creations, builds them, and saves state. You edit the file to three servers. Second run: the tool compares, sees one server missing, plans one creation only. You run it again unchanged: the plan is empty, nothing happens. That empty plan is idempotency in action.

Common mistake: making manual console changes to resources the IaC tool manages. The real environment now differs from the template, which is called drift. On the next run the tool may silently undo the manual fix, or the fix is lost when the environment is rebuilt in another region. In a running system this shows up as a mysterious outage after a routine deployment. The cure is to make every change in the template, commit it, and let the pipeline apply it; secrets such as passwords belong in a secrets store referenced by the template, never typed into the file.

questions.prompt: A city library team uses a declarative IaC template that declares four managed message queues and one database. Step 1: On the first run, the tool finds none of these resources in the cloud. It plans five creations, builds them, and saves a state record. Step 2: An engineer edits the template to also declare one load balancer, then commits the change to version control. Step 3: On the next run, the tool compares the template with its state record and with the real cloud. What does its plan contain? Step 4: The team runs the same template a third time with no edits, and the plan is empty. Which choice correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: It plans nothing, because the state record already shows that a deployment succeeded.
It plans to create a second copy of all six declared resources, because the template was run again.
It plans to delete and recreate all five existing resources, then create the load balancer, so that everything matches the new template.
It plans exactly one creation, the load balancer, because that is the only difference between the template and what already exists.
questions.why: A declarative tool compares the template with its state record and the real cloud, then plans only the differences, so the only thing it creates is the missing load balancer.

questions.prompt: A logistics company writes a file that says only: "three virtual machines and one private network should exist." The tool then works out on its own which steps to take. What style of infrastructure as code (IaC) is this?
choices: Declarative, because the file states the desired end result and the tool decides the steps.
Configuration management, because any file that names virtual machines is installing software inside them.
Version control, because the file is machine-readable and can be tracked over time.
Imperative, because the file lists the order in which resources must be created.
questions.why: A declarative template describes the end result and leaves the steps to the tool, while an imperative script lists the steps themselves.

questions.prompt: A clinic's IaC template creates a database that needs an administrator password. Following good IaC practice, where should that password be kept?
choices: In a comment at the top of the template, so that reviewers can see it during code review.
In a secrets store, with the template only referencing it rather than containing it.
Entered by hand in the cloud console after each build, so that it never touches any file.
Typed directly into the template, so that the build always has the password it needs.
questions.why: Secrets belong in a secrets store that the template references, never typed into the template file that sits in version control.

questions.prompt: During an incident at an online shop, an engineer opens an extra firewall port by hand in the cloud console. That firewall is a resource managed by the team's IaC tool, and the template was not changed. A week later a routine deployment runs the template. What is the most likely result?
choices: The tool records the manual port as part of the template, so the change becomes permanent.
The real environment has drifted from the template, so the run may silently undo the manual port and cause an outage.
Nothing happens, because idempotency means the tool never changes resources that already exist.
The deployment fails immediately and refuses to run until someone deletes the firewall.
questions.why: A manual change that is not in the template creates drift, and the next run can revert it to match the template, which explains why the fix should have been made in the template and committed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who likes clicking in the console why the team should build its cloud environment with infrastructure as code. Cover declarative templates and idempotency, and name at least one limit or tradeoff of the approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Infrastructure as code means we write our networks, machines and permissions into template files kept in version control, and a tool builds the cloud to match. Our templates are declarative: they describe the end state, and the tool compares that with its saved state and the real cloud, then changes only the differences. That makes runs idempotent, so applying the same file twice does nothing extra, and we can rebuild identical environments for test, production or disaster recovery. Every change gets reviewed and can be rolled back. The tradeoff is discipline and upfront effort: you have to learn the tool, protect the state record, and stop making console edits, because a manual change creates drift that the next run may overwrite.
