questions.why: A trace follows one request as it moves through multiple services and shows how much time each one took, which metrics, logs, and baselines do not do.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm reviews monitoring data for a virtual server that hosts its weekly route-planning report. For the past six weeks, CPU utilization has stayed around 4% and has never gone above 10%. What does right-sizing suggest the team should do?
choices: Add a second server of the same size so the report has spare capacity for peaks
Leave it unchanged, because low CPU proves the server is healthy and correctly sized
Move the workload to a smaller server, because its size far exceeds what it actually uses
Lower the CPU alert threshold to 5% so the team is notified about the low usage
questions.why: Right-sizing means matching resource size to real use, so a server that sits at about 4% CPU for weeks can be made smaller to save money.

questions.prompt: A streaming service's dashboard shows average response time for its search feature at 180 ms, close to normal, yet many users complain that searches sometimes take several seconds. The team only watches the average. What is the most likely reason the dashboard looks fine?
choices: The average hides the slow tail of requests; a percentile such as p95 would reveal it
The baseline was recorded under typical load, so it automatically includes the slow searches
The servers' CPU must be overloaded, and CPU problems never appear in latency metrics
Logs cannot record slow requests, so complaints cannot show up in any monitoring data
questions.why: Averages blend a few very slow requests in with many fast ones, so the slow tail that users feel stays hidden unless you watch a percentile like p95, the value 95% of requests finish faster than.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use monitoring data to find and fix a performance problem in a cloud service. Include why baselines and percentiles matter, and name one limit or tradeoff of monitoring.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I'd make sure we collect three kinds of signals. Metrics, like CPU and latency, give the trend over time. Logs tell us what happened at a given moment. Traces show which service inside a request was slow. Before alerting on anything, I'd record a baseline of normal behavior so thresholds mean something. I'd alert on p95 or p99 latency, not just the average, because the average can look fine while one user in twenty waits seconds. When an alert fires, I'd check whether resources like CPU are saturated. If they aren't, I'd follow traces to the slow dependency, fix it, and confirm the metrics return to baseline. The same data shows over-provisioned resources we can shrink to save money. The tradeoff is that more monitoring costs money and attention. Collecting and storing lots of data isn't free, and too many noisy alerts cause alert fatigue, so people start ignoring real problems.
rubricPoints: Names metrics, logs and traces and what each one is good for.
Explains that a baseline defines normal so thresholds and alerts are meaningful.
Explains that percentiles such as p95 reveal slow requests that averages hide.
Describes tracing a slowdown to its bottleneck and confirming the fix against the baseline.
Mentions using utilization data for right-sizing or cost optimization.
Names a limit, such as monitoring cost, data volume or alert fatigue from noisy thresholds.

suggested.rationale: Investigating a slow API after a deploy makes the learner read performance signals, compare them to normal behavior and find the bottleneck, which is exactly the monitoring-and-analysis skill.

lessons.plain: A deployment is the act of putting new or changed resources and software into a cloud environment, such as starting servers from a template or releasing a new app version. Sometimes it fails or half-works. Diagnosing a deployment problem means finding out exactly which step broke and why, instead of trying random fixes. Think of it like a recipe that went wrong. Rather than throwing everything out, you check which step failed. Was an ingredient missing, was the oven too small, or was the instruction misread? Fix that one step, then try again.
lessons.guessPrompt: A template that creates three new virtual servers fails with an error mentioning a limit in that region, even though the same template worked last month in a different region. What do you think is the most likely cause, and would simply retrying help?
lessons.teach:
A deployment problem is any failure that happens while creating or changing cloud resources or releasing software. A deployment often uses a template, which is a file describing the resources you want. Writing infrastructure as files like this is called infrastructure as code.

The most reliable way to diagnose a failure is to find the stage that broke. There are four stages to check. Validation is when the template is checked for syntax and allowed values. Provisioning is when the provider actually creates resources. Configuration is when software and settings are applied. Startup is when a health check confirms the service responds. A health check is an automatic probe that asks whether the service is working.

Each stage has typical causes. Validation fails on typos or unsupported options. Provisioning fails when you exceed a quota, which is a provider-set cap on resources such as processor cores per region. It can also fail when the deploy identity lacks permission, or when a size or service is not offered in that region. Configuration fails on wrong versions or missing dependencies. Startup fails on bad settings or ports. The deploy identity is the account or role the tooling acts as.

Worked example: a deployment of three 4-core servers fails. First, read the error, which says the core quota was exceeded. That places the failure at the provisioning stage. Next, check usage. The limit is 16 cores, 12 are already used, and the request needs 3 × 4 = 12 more. That totals 24, which is over 16. To fix it, request a quota increase, choose a smaller size, or deploy to another region. Then redeploy and confirm the health check passes.

A common mistake is retrying blindly, or changing several things at once. If you change several things together, you never learn what actually fixed it. Compare against the last known good deployment and change one variable at a time. If production is hurting, roll back first and diagnose afterward. A rollback means returning to the previous working version.

In a running system, a failed deployment can leave orphaned resources that still cost money. It can also leave a mix of old and new versions, so the environment ends up in an inconsistent state that needs cleanup.

questions.prompt: A small online bookshop uses infrastructure as code (resources described in a template file) to release a new version of its web app. The deployment reports a failure, and an engineer works through it. Step 1: read the log. The template check passed. The provider created both virtual machines and the load balancer. The install script finished and installed the correct runtime version. Then the automatic health check (a probe asking whether the service responds) got no answer on port 8080. The app's settings file tells it to listen on port 8000. Step 2: ______. Step 3: change only the port setting so the app and the health check agree, redeploy, and confirm the health check passes. Which statement correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Place the failure at the startup stage, because everything earlier succeeded and a bad port setting stopped the service from answering its health check
Place the failure at the configuration stage, because a dependency must be missing from the install
Place the failure at the provisioning stage, because the load balancer must have exceeded a regional quota
Place the failure at the validation stage, because a port mismatch is a typo in the template
questions.why: Validation, provisioning and configuration all succeeded, and the fault is a wrong port setting that a health check exposed, which is a typical startup-stage failure.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's cloud region has a quota (a provider-set cap) of 32 processor cores. It already uses 20 cores. A new template requests two servers with 8 cores each. Which outcome should the team expect?
choices: The deployment succeeds, because 16 new cores is under the 32-core limit
The deployment fails at provisioning, because 20 + 16 = 36 cores, which is over the 32-core quota
The deployment succeeds but then fails its health check at startup
The deployment fails at validation, because the template asks for too many cores
questions.why: Quota checks count existing usage plus the new request, and 36 exceeds 32, so the provider refuses to create the resources during provisioning.

questions.prompt: After a failed deployment, an engineer changes the server image version, the region and the server size all at once, then redeploys. This time it works. What is the main problem with this approach?
choices: Changing the region always causes a validation error, so the success must be temporary
The engineer should have retried the original deployment several times before changing anything
Nothing is wrong, because a working deployment proves the original fault is understood
The team cannot tell which change fixed the fault, so they should have compared against the last known good deployment and changed one variable at a time
questions.why: Changing several things together hides the actual cause, which is why the method is to change one variable at a time against a known good baseline.

questions.prompt: An insurance company releases a new version of its customer portal. Within minutes, customers in production start getting errors and cannot log in. What should the team do first?
choices: Start diagnosing which of the four stages failed while customers keep seeing errors
Retry the same deployment until it succeeds
Delete all resources in the region to clear any orphaned resources
Roll back to the previous working version, then diagnose the failure afterward
questions.why: When production is hurting, the rule is to restore the last working version first and investigate once users are no longer affected.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would work out why a cloud deployment failed, using the idea of deployment stages. Include one tradeoff, such as when to roll back versus keep digging.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by reading the actual error and asking which stage failed. The stages are validation (is the template valid?), provisioning (could the provider create the resources?), configuration (did software and settings apply?) and startup (does the health check pass?). The stage narrows the causes. Provisioning failures usually come from three things: a quota limit, missing permissions on the deploy identity, or a size or service not offered in that region. Configuration failures point to wrong versions or dependencies. I compare against the last known good deployment and change one thing at a time, so I know what fixed it. I also clean up any half-created resources. The tradeoff is this: if users are affected, I roll back first to restore service, even though that can hide the evidence and delay finding the root cause. If nothing is live yet, I can take time to diagnose properly.
rubricPoints: Reads the actual error message before acting.
Locates the failure by stage: validation, provisioning, configuration or startup.
Names typical causes such as quota limits, missing deploy permissions, regional availability or wrong versions.
Compares with the last known good state and changes one variable at a time.
Weighs rolling back to restore service against keeping the broken state for diagnosis.
Mentions cleaning up partial or orphaned resources.

suggested.rationale: This mission has the learner handle a failed release by restoring service through rollback and then diagnosing and fixing the cause, which is the core loop of resolving deployment problems.

lessons.plain: Cloud network troubleshooting is figuring out why one thing in the cloud cannot talk to another. A cloud network is built from software settings: private address ranges, routing rules and firewalls. Any one of them can quietly block traffic. Instead of guessing, you follow the path a message takes from sender to receiver and check every gate along the way. Think of a parcel that never arrived. You don't reprint the label at random. You check whether the address was right, whether a road existed, whether a gate was locked, and whether anyone was home to sign for it.
lessons.guessPrompt: You try to connect to a cloud server. In one case the attempt hangs for 30 seconds and then gives up. In another case it fails instantly with 'connection refused.' Which failure points more toward a firewall silently dropping your traffic, and why?
lessons.teach:
Troubleshooting cloud connectivity means tracing a packet's path from source to destination, hop by hop, and checking each control that could drop it. A packet is a small chunk of network traffic.

A few terms first. A virtual network (AWS calls it a VPC, Azure a VNet) is your private address space in the cloud. It is divided into subnets, which are smaller address ranges. A route table tells traffic leaving a subnet where to go next. Typical next stops are an internet gateway, the door to the public internet, or a NAT gateway, which lets private servers reach outward without being reachable from outside.

Two filters sit on the path. A security group is a stateful firewall attached to an instance (a virtual server). Stateful means replies to allowed traffic are let back in automatically. A network ACL is a stateless filter on the whole subnet. Stateless means it checks inbound and outbound traffic separately, so reply traffic needs its own rule.

Check in this order: does the name resolve to an address, is there a route, do the filters allow the port in both directions, and is the service listening? Each check rules out a whole class of causes.

Two symptoms help. A timeout usually means something silently dropped the packet, such as a filter or a missing route. 'Connection refused' means the packet arrived but nothing was listening on that port.

Here is an example. A web server times out on port 443 from the internet. First, it has a public IP. Second, the route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 (all addresses) to the internet gateway. Third, the security group allows inbound 443. Fourth, the network ACL allows inbound 443, but outbound only to port 443. Replies go to the client's ephemeral port, a temporary high-numbered port, so they are dropped. The fix is to allow outbound ephemeral ports in the ACL.

A common mistake is opening the security group to all traffic when the real blocker is a route or an ACL. That widens the attack surface and does not fix the outage. Meanwhile, failed health checks keep pulling servers out of the load balancer's rotation.

questions.prompt: A regional bakery chain runs an inventory server in a private subnet. The server has no public IP. It times out when it tries to download updates from a supplier's website on port 443. An engineer traces the path, and one step of the trace is missing. Step 1, name resolution: the supplier's name resolves to an address, so DNS is not the cause. Step 2, route: [missing]. Step 3, security group: it allows outbound 443, and because it is stateful the replies are let back in automatically. Step 4, network ACL: it allows outbound 443 and inbound ephemeral ports, so traffic is allowed in both directions. Conclusion: the route was the fault, and fixing it restores the downloads. Which finding belongs in Step 2?
choices: There is no route problem, but the timeout means nothing is listening on the supplier's port 443, so the supplier must start its service.
The subnet's route table has no route for 0.0.0.0/0, so outbound traffic has nowhere to go. Adding a 0.0.0.0/0 route to a NAT gateway fixes it.
The route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway as expected, so routing is fine and the engineer moves on to the filters.
The route is missing, but the quicker fix is to open the server's security group to all inbound traffic so replies can return.
questions.why: The conclusion says the route was at fault, and a private server with no public IP reaches outward through a NAT gateway, so the missing finding is a missing 0.0.0.0/0 route to a NAT gateway.

questions.prompt: A firm's app server sends requests out through a subnet filter. The filter allows the outbound traffic, but the replies never come back until a separate inbound rule is added for them. Which kind of filter behaves this way, and why?
choices: A route table, because it drops any reply traffic that it has no route for.
An internet gateway, because it blocks replies coming from the public internet.
A network ACL, because it is stateless and checks inbound and outbound traffic separately.
A security group, because it is stateful and checks each direction on its own.
questions.why: A network ACL is stateless, so reply traffic needs its own rule, while a stateful security group lets replies to allowed traffic back in automatically.

questions.prompt: A clinic's reporting tool tries to connect to a database server on port 5432. It immediately gets 'connection refused' instead of waiting and timing out. What does this symptom most likely tell you?
choices: The packet reached the server, but nothing is listening on port 5432.
The route table has no route to the database server's subnet.
The database's name did not resolve to an address.
A network ACL silently dropped the packet before it reached the server.
questions.why: 'Connection refused' means the packet arrived but no service was listening on that port, while a silent drop by a filter or a missing route usually shows up as a timeout.

questions.prompt: At an online bookshop, web servers behind a load balancer start timing out on port 8443. Without tracing the path, an engineer opens the servers' security group to all traffic from anywhere. The real blocker is a network ACL rule. What is the most likely result?
choices: The outage continues and the attack surface is wider, while failed health checks keep pulling servers out of the load balancer's rotation.
The outage is fixed, because a security group rule overrides a network ACL rule.
The outage is fixed, but only for traffic that comes from inside the virtual network.
Nothing changes at all, because security groups only filter outbound traffic.
questions.why: Opening the security group does not touch the ACL that is actually dropping packets, so the outage continues, more exposure is added, and health checks keep failing.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would work out why a cloud server is unreachable. Cover why the order of checks matters, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach, such as stateful versus stateless filters.
lessons.modelAnswer: I trace the path a packet takes instead of changing settings at random. First, does the name resolve to the right address? Next, does the subnet's route table send traffic where it needs to go, for example to an internet gateway for public access or a NAT gateway for outbound-only access? Then I check both filters. The security group is stateful, so if inbound is allowed, replies are allowed. The network ACL is stateless, so I must also allow reply traffic outbound, usually on the high ephemeral ports. Finally, I confirm the service is actually listening. A timeout points to something dropping packets. 'Refused' means the traffic arrived but no service answered. One tradeoff is that loosening rules can make the symptom disappear while creating a security hole, so I fix the exact rule at fault and nothing wider.
rubricPoints: Follows the packet path in order: name resolution, routing, filters, then the listening service.
Explains that route tables decide the next hop, such as an internet gateway or a NAT gateway.
Distinguishes a stateful security group from a stateless network ACL that needs return-traffic rules.
Uses timeout versus connection refused to narrow down where the fault is.
Warns against over-opening firewall rules as a fix, because it adds risk without finding the cause.

suggested.rationale: A virtual network path tracer would let the learner walk a packet through routes, security groups and ACLs and find the exact hop that drops it, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: A security incident is any event where someone may have gained access or power they should not have. Two common cloud cases are a leaked credential, meaning a password, access key or token that has escaped to somewhere others can see it, and privilege escalation, meaning an account getting more permissions than it was meant to have. Handling the incident means stopping the damage first, then finding out what happened and closing the gap. Think of a lost house key. You change the lock before you search for the key, and then you check whether anything was taken.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer accidentally pushes a cloud access key to a public code repository and deletes the file one minute later. Is the key safe now, and what is the very first thing you would do?
lessons.teach:
Responding to a leaked credential or a privilege escalation follows a fixed order. First contain, then investigate, then repair and prevent. A credential is anything that proves identity to a system, such as an access key, an API token or a password. Privilege escalation is when an identity gains permissions beyond what it was granted. A common route is an account allowed to edit its own permission policy, or to attach an administrator policy to itself.

Containment comes first because a leaked secret can be copied by automated scanners within seconds. Deleting it from where it leaked does nothing about copies that already exist. Revocation means disabling the credential so the cloud provider rejects it. Rotation means issuing a replacement and updating the applications that use it.

Worked example. An access key appears in a public repository. Step one: revoke that key at the identity service. Step two: create a new key, store it in a secrets manager (a managed vault that hands secrets to applications at runtime), and redeploy the apps that need it. Step three: read the audit logs, which are records of every API call with who made it and when, and filter for the old key. Step four: look for signs of persistence. Persistence means anything an attacker leaves behind to get back in, such as new users, extra keys, new roles or changed policies. Also look for escalation, such as an administrator policy suddenly attached. Remove each one. Step five: fix the root cause. Apply least privilege, meaning each identity gets only the permissions it needs. Add secret scanning to the code pipeline.

A common mistake is rotating the key, or deleting the commit, and stopping there. If the attacker already created a second key or an admin role, they keep access after the original key dies. Meanwhile the running system looks normal while unexpected resources run up costs or data quietly leaves.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs a nightly billing job under its own service identity. At 01:40 an alert shows that this identity attached an administrator policy to itself. The on-call engineer responds in this order. Step 1: disable the job identity's token and detach the administrator policy, so the provider now rejects that identity's calls. Step 2: (missing). Step 3: using what was found in Step 2, delete one extra access key and one new role that were created at 01:52, and undo a policy change that had made a storage bucket publicly readable. Step 4: change the job identity so it can no longer edit its own permission policy, and limit it to reading the billing database only. What is the missing Step 2?
choices: Read the audit logs, filtered for the job identity's API calls from 01:40 onward, to see everything it did with the extra permissions.
Add secret scanning to the code pipeline so that tokens are caught before they are committed.
Re-attach the administrator policy for a short time so the job can finish tonight's billing run.
Redeploy the billing job with a fresh token and close the incident, because the administrator policy is already gone.
questions.why: Step 3 removes specific leftovers like an extra key, a new role and a changed policy, and those can only be found by investigating the audit logs for that identity's actions after it escalated.

questions.prompt: Which of these situations is an example of privilege escalation?
choices: A developer's password is pasted into a public chat channel by mistake.
An access key is replaced with a new one and the applications are updated to use it.
A storage bucket is deleted by an administrator who was allowed to delete it.
A deployment account that was only allowed to update servers edits its own permission policy to grant itself full administrator rights.
questions.why: Privilege escalation means an identity gains permissions beyond what it was granted, and editing its own policy to become an administrator is a common route.

questions.prompt: A university IT team finds that the password for a research API token was posted on a public wiki page about two hours ago. What should they do first?
choices: Read the audit logs to find out whether anyone has used the token yet.
Edit the wiki page to remove the token so no one else can see it.
Add secret scanning to the pipeline so this cannot happen again.
Revoke the token at the identity service so the provider rejects it.
questions.why: Containment comes first, and removing the token from the wiki does nothing about copies that may already exist, so it must be revoked so it stops working.

questions.prompt: A media startup's API key leaked in a public code repository. Within 15 minutes the team rotated the key and deleted the commit, then closed the incident. Five days later the bill shows 30 unfamiliar virtual machines running. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Rotating a key never disables the old key, so the attacker is still using the original one.
The new key was stored in a secrets manager, which exposes it to the public.
The attacker used the leaked key to create persistence, such as a second key or a new role, before it was rotated, and still has access.
The deleted commit was restored from history, so the original key is working again.
questions.why: Stopping at rotation skips checking the audit logs for persistence, so a second key or admin role created by the attacker keeps working after the original key dies and can quietly run up costs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would respond if a cloud access key leaked and you suspect it was used to escalate privileges. Include why the order of steps matters and one limit of simply rotating the key.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I would revoke the leaked key immediately, because automated scanners can copy a public secret within seconds. Removing it from the repository does not undo those copies. Next I would issue a replacement through a secrets manager and redeploy the apps that depend on it, so the service keeps running. Then I would search the audit logs for every call the old key made. I would look for persistence and escalation: new users, extra keys, new roles, or an administrator policy attached to an account that never had one. I would remove each of those. The limit of just rotating is that it only kills the one credential I know about. If the attacker already granted themselves another key or a stronger role, they still get in. Finally I would fix the cause: tighten permissions to least privilege so no identity can edit its own policy, and add secret scanning to the pipeline.
rubricPoints: Contain first by revoking or disabling the leaked credential, not just deleting it from where it leaked.
Rotate by issuing a replacement and updating the applications that depend on it.
Use audit logs to trace what the compromised identity actually did.
Hunt for persistence and escalation such as new keys, users, roles or attached admin policies, and remove them.
Fix the root cause with least privilege and secret handling such as a secrets manager or scanning.
Recognise that rotation alone fails if the attacker has already created other ways back in.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning through the correct order of containment, log investigation and cleanup in an exam-style scenario, and no single existing mission covers revocation plus escalation hunting end to end.

lessons.plain: Three background services keep a network usable. DNS works like a phone book: it turns a name such as shop.example.com into the numeric address computers actually use. DHCP works like a front desk handing each new arrival a room number: it gives a machine its address and tells it where to find other services. NTP works like a shared wall clock: it keeps every machine's time in agreement. When one of these breaks, the error usually appears somewhere else, as a login failure or a site that 'is down.' Fixing them means reading the symptom pattern to see which service is really at fault.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web app works when you type its numeric IP address into the browser but fails when you type its name. Which do you think is more likely broken: the network path to the server, or the lookup that turns the name into an address? Why?
lessons.teach:
DNS (Domain Name System) translates names like api.example.com into IP addresses, the numeric addresses machines use to find each other. DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) gives a machine its IP address, its gateway (the router it sends outside traffic through), and the addresses of its DNS servers. It hands these out on a time-limited loan called a lease. NTP (Network Time Protocol) keeps machine clocks synchronised to a trusted time source. Their failures surface elsewhere, so you diagnose by the pattern of symptoms.

A DNS fault looks like this: reaching a host by IP works, but reaching it by name fails with errors such as 'could not resolve host.' Common causes are a wrong record, the wrong DNS server configured, or a private zone (internal-only names) that is not linked to the virtual network. Another cause is a stale cached answer. TTL (time to live) is the number of seconds a resolver may reuse an answer before asking again.

A DHCP fault looks like this: new machines get no address, get a self-assigned 169.254.x.x address, or get an address with no gateway, while existing machines keep working until their leases renew. Causes include an exhausted address pool in the subnet and wrong DHCP options, the extra settings such as the DNS server address.

An NTP fault shows up as clock skew, a gap between a machine's clock and real time. Logins fail with 'token expired,' TLS certificates seem 'not yet valid,' and logs appear out of order. Causes include blocked UDP port 123 or an unreachable time source.

Worked example: after a migration, new VMs cannot reach the database but old ones can. Step 1: from a new VM, ping the database by IP. It works, so routing is fine. Step 2: look up the database name. It fails, so the fault is in DNS. Step 3: check which DNS server the VM uses. It is a retired server. Step 4: the VM learned that address from the DHCP options, which still point to the old server. Old VMs work only because their leases have not renewed. Correct the option, renew the leases, and confirm the name resolves.

Common mistake: you change a DNS record, clients still reach the old address, and you assume the change failed and edit it again. Usually the old answer is just cached until its TTL expires. Lower the TTL before a planned change. Because so many services depend on these three, one fault can look like a site-wide outage, and unnoticed clock skew can lock every user out of authentication.

questions.prompt: A logistics company scales its web tier from 12 to 45 virtual machines in one subnet during a sales event. Step 1: the 33 new VMs show self-assigned 169.254.x.x addresses and cannot reach anything, while the original 12 VMs keep serving traffic normally. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: compare how many addresses the subnet's DHCP pool can hand out with how many are already leased, and find the pool is full. Step 4: move the new VMs to a larger subnet (or enlarge the pool), then confirm they receive a real address and a gateway. Which choice is the missing Step 2?
choices: Conclude this is a DNS fault, because the new VMs cannot reach other hosts by name, and check the DNS records for the web tier.
Conclude the original 12 VMs are also broken but hiding it, and restart them so they pick up fresh settings from the network.
Conclude this is a DHCP fault, because the new VMs never received a proper address; the old VMs still work only because their leases have not come up for renewal.
Conclude this is an NTP fault, because the new VMs' clocks are probably skewed, and check whether UDP port 123 is blocked.
questions.why: A self-assigned 169.254.x.x address on new machines, while existing ones still work, is the DHCP pattern. Existing machines are unaffected until their leases renew, which is why the next step is to check the pool.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a media firm changes the DNS record for files.mediaco.net to point at a new server. The record's TTL (time to live) is 86400 seconds, which is 24 hours. Two hours later, some users still reach the old server. What is the best explanation and response?
choices: The users' clocks are skewed, so they see an old copy of the record; the engineer should check that UDP port 123 is open.
The change failed to save, so the engineer should edit the record again until all users reach the new server.
Resolvers are still reusing the cached old answer, which they may do for up to 24 hours; wait it out, and lower the TTL before future planned changes.
The users' DHCP leases are pointing them at the old server, so every user's lease must be renewed before the record can take effect.
questions.why: A changed record can keep returning its old value until each cached answer's TTL runs out, so editing the record again does not help.

questions.prompt: At an insurance company, users of an internal app suddenly see 'token expired' errors at login, even straight after signing in. Admins also notice that the app's log entries appear out of order. The day before, the security team tightened the firewall rules. What is the most likely cause?
choices: A private DNS zone is not linked to the app's virtual network, so internal names fail to resolve.
The DNS record for the app points at the wrong IP address, so users are reaching the wrong server.
The DHCP address pool in the app's subnet is exhausted, so the app servers have no valid address.
The new firewall rules block UDP port 123, so the servers cannot reach their time source and their clocks have drifted.
questions.why: 'Token expired' errors and out-of-order logs are signs of clock skew, and blocking UDP port 123 stops NTP from keeping clocks synchronised.

questions.prompt: A retailer creates a new virtual network for its reporting VMs. From a reporting VM, a ping to 10.20.4.15 works, but connecting to db.internal.retail fails with 'could not resolve host.' VMs in the company's original virtual network resolve that same name without any problem. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Routing between the virtual networks is broken, so the reporting VM cannot reach the database server.
The reporting VMs have clock skew, so the database server is rejecting their connections.
The DHCP pool is exhausted, so the reporting VMs never received an IP address.
The private DNS zone holding internal.retail names is not linked to the new virtual network.
questions.why: Reaching the host by IP works but reaching it by name fails, which is a DNS fault, and an internal-only zone that is not linked to the new network fits it exactly.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell whether an outage is really caused by DNS, DHCP, or NTP rather than by the application itself, and name one limit or tradeoff, such as how DNS caching (TTL) affects how fast a fix takes effect.
lessons.modelAnswer: These three services are dependencies, so their failures show up as someone else's error. First I test by IP versus by name. If the IP works and the name fails, it's DNS: a wrong record, the wrong resolver, an unlinked private zone, or a stale cached answer. If new machines get no address, a 169.254 address, or no gateway while old machines are fine, it's DHCP: the pool may be exhausted, or the options may point to the wrong DNS server. Old machines keep working until their leases renew. If logins fail with 'token expired' or certificates seem not yet valid, I compare clocks for NTP skew and check that UDP 123 is reachable. The tradeoff with DNS is TTL. A long TTL cuts lookup traffic, but fixes spread slowly because clients keep the cached answer until it expires. So I lower the TTL before planned changes and don't keep re-editing a record that is only cached.
rubricPoints: Defines what DNS, DHCP and NTP each provide.
Uses the IP-works-but-name-fails test to identify DNS faults.
Recognises DHCP symptoms such as no address, 169.254 addresses, or only new machines failing.
Links authentication or certificate errors to clock skew from NTP problems.
Explains that TTL caching delays DNS fixes and is a tradeoff against lookup load.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine simulates DNS, DHCP or NTP failures, so reasoning through exam-style symptom scenarios best builds the skill of matching each symptom pattern to the failing service.

lessons.plain: A cloud misconfiguration is a setting that is wrong even though nothing is physically broken. The servers run and the network works, but one setting does not match what the system needs. Examples include a firewall rule on the wrong port, a storage area left open to the public, or a permission that is too narrow or too broad. Think of a house with sound walls where the front door was installed with the lock on the outside. Fixing it means finding which setting differs from what was intended, correcting that one setting, and making sure it stays fixed.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web app sat behind a load balancer and worked fine yesterday. This morning every request fails, yet all the servers are running and their logs show no errors. Someone changed settings last night. Where would you look first, and why?
lessons.teach:
A misconfiguration is a cloud setting whose value differs from what the workload needs. Common ones are an open or closed port in a security group (a virtual firewall attached to a resource), a storage bucket (a managed file store) readable by anyone, an identity policy (rules saying who may do what) that grants too little or too much, a wrong instance size or region, and a load balancer health check (a periodic test request that decides whether a server gets traffic) aimed at the wrong place.

The reliable method is to compare actual settings against a baseline. A baseline is the recorded, approved configuration. Configuration drift is the gap that grows when people change things by hand. Audit logs (records of who changed what, and when) show recent changes. Infrastructure as code means settings are kept in version-controlled files, so the baseline is easy to read and compare.

Worked example. Users get errors, but the servers are healthy. Step 1: the load balancer reports every target as unhealthy. Step 2: the health check probes port 8080. Step 3: the app listens on port 80, and the code files say the check should use port 80. Step 4: the audit log shows someone edited the check last night. Step 5: set the check back to port 80, then watch the targets turn healthy and traffic return. Step 6: put the same change in the code files and redeploy, so drift does not come back.

A common mistake is fixing by widening. Someone opens all ports or grants an administrator role "to see if it helps." The symptom may vanish, but now there is a security hole and the real cause is still unknown.

In a running system, a misconfiguration can cause a full outage, as in the example. It can also cause a silent data exposure that nobody notices until it is exploited. A fix made only in the console is likely to be overwritten by the next automated deployment. Treat a change as complete only when it is recorded in the baseline.

questions.prompt: At a shipping company, a nightly reporting job suddenly fails to save its output to a storage bucket (a managed file store). The team's settings are kept as infrastructure as code (version-controlled files that record the approved configuration). Step 1: the job's log shows an "access denied" error each time it tries to write to the bucket. Step 2: ______. Step 3: the audit log (a record of who changed what, and when) shows a colleague edited that policy on Tuesday while tidying up permissions. Step 4: the team restores the write permission through the code files and redeploys, and the next run saves its output. Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Move the job to a larger instance size in case it is running out of resources
Temporarily give the job's identity an administrator role to see whether the error goes away
Open all ports in the job server's security group so nothing can block the connection
Compare the job's live identity policy with the version in the code files and find that the write permission is missing from the live copy
questions.why: Comparing the actual setting against the recorded baseline pinpoints the exact difference, the missing write permission, which the audit log then explains.

questions.prompt: A small retailer set up its cloud network carefully six months ago and recorded that setup as approved. Since then, several staff have changed firewall rules and server sizes by hand in the console, and nobody updated the record. What is the name for the growing gap between the recorded setup and what is actually running?
choices: An audit log
A health check
Configuration drift
A baseline
questions.why: Configuration drift is the gap that grows between the approved baseline and the live settings when people make manual changes.

questions.prompt: At a travel booking firm, customers cannot reach a new booking page. An engineer opens the needed port in the security group (a virtual firewall attached to a resource) using the web console, and the page starts working. The next morning the page is unreachable again and the port is closed. The firm deploys all its settings automatically from version-controlled code files every night. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The booking page crashed overnight and closed the port itself
Someone deleted the audit log, which undid the change
The nightly deployment reapplied the code files, which still had the port closed, overwriting the console-only fix
The security group expires opened ports after a fixed time
questions.why: A fix made only in the console is not part of the baseline, so the next automated deployment restores the old value from the code files.

questions.prompt: At a clinic's patient portal, an app server cannot read files it needs. An engineer grants the server's identity a full administrator role "to see if it helps," and the error disappears. Why is this a poor way to handle the problem?
choices: Administrator roles always make the app run more slowly
It is fine as a permanent fix as long as the error is gone
It creates a security hole by granting far more access than needed, and the actual misconfiguration is still unidentified
It automatically causes configuration drift to be recorded in the baseline
questions.why: Fixing by widening hides the symptom while adding excess access, and leaves the real cause unknown.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would track down and fix a suspected cloud misconfiguration. Include why you would not just loosen permissions or open ports until the problem goes away, and name one limit of relying on a baseline.
lessons.modelAnswer: A misconfiguration is a setting that doesn't match what the system needs, even though the hardware and software are fine. First I find which component the symptom points to, like a load balancer marking everything unhealthy. Then I compare its live settings to our baseline, the approved config kept in our infrastructure-as-code files. I also check the audit log for recent changes. When I find the one setting that differs, I correct that single value and confirm the symptom clears. Then I commit the same fix to code so the next deployment doesn't undo it. I won't open all ports or grant admin rights to test, because that hides the cause and creates a security exposure. One limit is that a baseline only helps if it is correct and current. If the baseline itself holds the bad value, or people make untracked manual changes, the comparison can mislead you.
rubricPoints: Defines a misconfiguration as a wrong setting, not broken infrastructure.
Compares live settings to a baseline and checks audit logs for recent changes.
Changes only the specific faulty setting and verifies that the symptom clears.
Records the fix in the baseline or infrastructure as code to prevent drift.
Warns against over-broad fixes such as opening all ports or granting admin rights.
Names a limit, such as a baseline that is wrong or out of date.

suggested.rationale: Spotting which setting is wrong among plausible symptoms is mostly a reasoning skill, best practised on exam-style broken-deployment scenarios rather than in a single existing mission.

lessons.plain: Automation in cloud operations means handing a repeated chore, such as building servers, patching them, or checking their health, to software that does it the same way every time. Instead of an engineer clicking through the same 30 steps each week, the steps are written down once as a file that a tool can run. Think of a bread machine: you measure the recipe once, press start, and you get the same loaf every time without standing over the oven. Automation saves time, but mostly it removes the small human slips that happen when people repeat boring work.
lessons.guessPrompt: You must apply the same security setting to 200 cloud servers every month. What could go wrong if a person does it by hand each time, and what would you want a tool to guarantee instead?
lessons.teach:
Automation means letting software carry out an operations task that a person would otherwise do by hand, such as creating servers, applying patches, rotating logs or checking health. Orchestration means coordinating many automated steps in the right order across many systems: create the network, then the database, then the app servers. Three common forms exist. A script is a file of commands run top to bottom. Infrastructure as code (IaC) is a set of text files describing the cloud resources you want, which a tool reads and builds. Configuration management is a tool that brings each server's settings to a described state.

Why it works: a computer runs the same steps the same way every time, so results are repeatable, fast and logged. The files can live in source control and be reviewed like any other code.

Two terms matter. Declarative means you describe the end state (three web servers, port 443 open) and the tool works out the steps. Imperative means you list each step yourself. Idempotent means running the automation twice gives the same result as running it once, because it changes only what is not already correct.

Worked example: every Monday an engineer logs into 40 virtual machines (VMs) to install updates and restart a service. Step 1, describe the goal once: package X at the latest version, service Y running. Step 2, test it on two staging VMs. Step 3, schedule it weekly. Step 4, on each run the tool checks every VM: 37 already match and are left alone, 3 are updated and restarted. Step 5, the output is logged for review. Hours of manual work become minutes, and no VM is skipped.

Common mistake: writing non-idempotent steps, such as "append this line to the config file," which adds a duplicate line on every run until the service breaks. A related mistake is still making manual quick fixes on automated servers. This causes configuration drift, where servers slowly stop matching the described state, and the next automated run overwrites the fix or behaves unpredictably. If automation owns a resource, change it through the automation.

questions.prompt: A game studio keeps an infrastructure as code (IaC) file in source control. IaC means text files that describe the cloud resources you want, which a tool reads and builds. The file is declarative: it states the end state, which is one virtual network, one load balancer and 6 game servers. Right now the cloud account already has the network, the load balancer and 4 game servers. An engineer runs the IaC tool. Trace: (a) The tool reads the file to learn the desired end state. (b) The tool compares that to what exists. The network and load balancer match, and 2 game servers are missing. (c) ______ (d) An hour later the engineer runs the tool again with no file changes, and it reports nothing to change. Which choice correctly fills step (c)?
choices: The tool creates 6 new game servers, so the account now holds 10 in total
The tool deletes all existing resources and rebuilds everything from scratch
The tool creates only the 2 missing game servers and leaves the rest untouched
The tool stops and asks the engineer to list each creation step in order
questions.why: A declarative, idempotent tool changes only what does not already match the described state, so it adds just the 2 missing servers, which is why the second run finds nothing to do.

questions.prompt: A logistics company is choosing how to write its cloud automation. Which description is an example of a declarative approach?
choices: An engineer typing each command into a console while following a written checklist
A scheduled job that reruns the same list of commands every night in a fixed order
A file stating that two web servers should exist with port 80 open, and the tool works out how to get there
A script that runs: create subnet, then open port 80, then launch server one, then launch server two
questions.why: Declarative means you describe the end state and the tool figures out the steps, while listing each step yourself is imperative.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain's nightly automation on its 8 point-of-sale servers includes the step "add this scheduled-task line to the end of the task file." The step has now run on 15 nights. What is the most likely state of each server, and what is the right fix?
choices: The file holds one copy, but only on the servers checked first; add more servers to the schedule
The file holds 15 copies of the line; rewrite the step to make sure the line is present once rather than appending it
The file holds one copy of the line, because automation always runs the same way; no fix is needed
The file is empty, because each run replaces the previous one; switch to running it by hand
questions.why: Appending is not idempotent, so every run adds another duplicate, and the fix is a step that changes the file only if the line is not already there.

questions.prompt: A university runs 12 servers whose settings are managed by a configuration management tool, meaning a tool that brings each server's settings to a described state. During an outage, an engineer logs into 2 of them and raises a timeout value by hand, without touching the automation files. What is the most likely result, and what should have been done?
choices: The tool learns from the manual change and copies the new timeout to the other 10 servers automatically
The next automated run sets the timeout back to the described value, so the change belongs in the automation files
The tool deletes the 2 servers because they no longer match, so they must be rebuilt by hand afterwards
Nothing happens to the 2 servers, because automation only acts on servers that have never been touched by hand
questions.why: Manual fixes on automated servers cause configuration drift, and the next run overwrites them, so a resource that automation owns should be changed through the automation.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why the team should automate a weekly manual task like patching and restarting servers, what idempotent and declarative mean in that context, and name one limit or tradeoff of automating it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Right now someone patches 40 VMs by hand each week. That is slow, and sooner or later someone skips a box or mistypes a command. If we write the desired state once, for example "this package at the latest version, this service running," a tool can apply it the same way to every server on a schedule and log what it did. That is declarative: we describe the end state and the tool works out the steps. It should also be idempotent, so running it again only fixes servers that are wrong and leaves correct ones alone. The tradeoff is that automation takes upfront effort to write and test, and a mistake in it spreads to every server at once. That is why we test on staging first. We also have to stop making manual fixes, or the servers drift away from what the automation expects.
rubricPoints: Defines automation as software performing a repeated operations task instead of a person.
Explains the benefit: repeatable, fast, logged and less human error.
Explains idempotent as safe to run repeatedly with the same result.
Distinguishes declarative (describe end state) from imperative (list steps).
Names a tradeoff, such as upfront effort, errors spreading to every server, or drift from manual changes.
Mentions testing on a small or staging set before running everywhere.

suggested.rationale: Writing a first script that replaces a manual health check is the most direct hands-on way to feel how a repeated operations chore becomes automation.

lessons.plain: Source control (also called version control) is a system that keeps every saved version of your code and configuration files, records who changed what and when, and lets several people work on the same files without overwriting each other. Think of it as a shared document with a perfect, permanent history: you can see every edit, compare any two versions, and go back to an earlier one if something breaks. Git is the most common source control tool. In cloud operations it is not just for application code; scripts, infrastructure templates and pipeline definitions live there too, so every change to your environment is tracked and reversible.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two engineers edit the same server configuration file on the same day, and the next morning the site is broken. Without any special tool, what two facts would you most want to know to fix it quickly, and how might a system that saves every version help you find them?
lessons.teach:
Source control is a tool that stores the full history of a set of files so a team can change them safely. Here are the core terms. A repository (repo) is the tracked project folder plus its history. A commit is a saved snapshot of changes with an author, a time and a message explaining why. A branch is a separate line of work that starts from an existing point, so you can experiment without touching the main line (usually called main). A merge brings a branch's commits back into another branch. A merge conflict happens when two branches changed the same lines differently and a person must choose the correct result. A pull request (or merge request) is a proposal to merge a branch that teammates review before it is accepted. A tag is a fixed label on one commit, such as v1.4, marking a release. A revert is a new commit that undoes an earlier one while keeping the history intact.

This works because every change is small, named and recorded, so you can find exactly which change caused a problem and undo just that change.

Worked example: Priya needs to raise a web server's timeout. She creates a branch called fix-timeout from main, edits the config file, and commits with the message "Raise timeout to 60s for slow uploads." She opens a pull request; a teammate reviews and approves it, and it is merged into main. The release is tagged v2.3. Next day errors rise. The team looks at the history, sees the timeout commit was the only change, and reverts it, returning to the previous behaviour in minutes.

A common mistake is committing secrets such as passwords or access keys into the repo. History is permanent, so even deleting the file later leaves the secret in old commits; it must be rotated. Use an ignore file (in Git, .gitignore) to keep secret and generated files out, and store secrets in a dedicated secrets manager. Skipping branches and reviews and committing straight to main means untested changes reach production with no second pair of eyes.

questions.prompt: At a regional hospital's IT team, Ana and Ben each create a branch from main. Ana's branch changes line 12 of backup-schedule.conf so nightly backups run at 01:00. Ben's branch changes the same line 12 to 03:00. Ana's pull request is reviewed and merged into main first. Here is what happens next. Step 1: Ben opens a pull request to merge his branch into main. Step 2: The tool reports a merge conflict, because both branches changed the same line in different ways. Step 3: ??? Step 4: Ben commits the resolved file with the message "Resolve backup time conflict: keep 03:00 per storage team." A teammate approves, and the branch is merged. What belongs in Step 3?
choices: Ben reverts Ana's merged commit so that his own change can merge in cleanly
The tool keeps whichever edit has the newer timestamp and completes the merge by itself
Ben tags both versions of the file, for example v3.0 and v3.1, so main can keep both times
Ben checks with Ana, picks the one correct time, and edits line 12 to hold only that value
questions.why: A merge conflict means two branches changed the same lines differently, so a person has to choose the correct result before the merge can finish.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company's operations team ships release 7.2 of its deployment scripts. They want a fixed label on the exact commit that went out, so they can find that commit months later. In source control, a commit is a saved snapshot of changes. Which feature gives them this fixed label?
choices: A pull request, which teammates review before merging
A merge, which brings one branch's commits into another
A branch, which is a separate line of work
A tag, which is a fixed label on one commit
questions.why: A tag is a fixed label on one commit, such as v7.2, and it is used to mark a release.

questions.prompt: An engineer at an online retailer commits a file called settings.env that contains a production database password. An hour later she notices and deletes the file in a new commit. What still needs to happen?
choices: Add settings.env to the ignore file; that alone fully protects the old password
Revert the commit that added the file, which wipes the password from history
Change (rotate) the password, since old commits still hold it, and use a secrets manager
Nothing more, because the deleting commit removed the password from the repo
questions.why: History is permanent, so the password is still readable in the old commit. The password must be rotated, and secrets belong in a dedicated secrets manager rather than in the repo.

questions.prompt: At a logistics firm, a change to a load balancer config made four commits ago is now causing failed health checks. The three commits made after it are working fine. The team wants to undo only the bad change and keep a complete record of what happened. What should they do?
choices: Revert that one commit, which adds a new commit undoing it and leaves history intact
Start a new branch from main and carry on working there instead of fixing main
Erase the repo's history back to before the bad commit and redo the later work
Tag the bad commit as broken so that future deployments skip over it
questions.why: A revert is a new commit that undoes one earlier commit without rewriting history, so the three good commits after it stay in place.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a new teammate how your team should use branches, commits, pull requests and tags when changing a cloud configuration file, and name one limit or risk of source control that they still need to watch out for.
lessons.modelAnswer: We keep our configs in a repository, which is the project plus its full history. To make a change, you create a branch off main so your work is isolated. You make small commits, each with a clear message saying why, so anyone can trace a change later. When ready, you open a pull request so a teammate reviews it before it is merged into main; that catches mistakes early. When we release, we tag the commit, like v2.3, so we know exactly what is running. If a release misbehaves, we revert the bad commit, which undoes it while keeping history. The limit: source control remembers everything forever, so if you commit a password it stays in history even after deletion and must be rotated. Keep secrets out with an ignore file and a secrets manager. Also, two branches editing the same lines cause merge conflicts that a person must resolve carefully.
rubricPoints: Defines a repository and commit as tracked history with author, time and message.
Explains branches isolate work and merges bring it back to main.
Describes pull requests as peer review before merging.
Mentions tags marking releases and revert to undo a bad change safely.
Names a limit such as secrets staying in history or merge conflicts needing manual resolution.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine has the learner drive source control directly, so explaining the branch, review, tag and revert workflow back in their own words is the strongest way to lock in the concepts the exam tests.

lessons.plain: A CI/CD pipeline is an automatic assembly line for software changes. Every time someone saves a change to the shared code, the pipeline picks it up, builds it, runs the tests, and, if everything passes, packages it and delivers it toward the live servers. Nobody has to remember the steps or run them by hand. Think of a car factory line: each station does one job, and a car that fails inspection at one station never reaches the showroom. The pipeline's value is that the same checks happen the same way every time, so mistakes are caught early and releases become routine instead of scary.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a team runs its tests by hand only when someone remembers, and a new team runs them automatically on every code change, which team do you think finds a bug sooner after it is written, and why?
lessons.teach:
A CI/CD pipeline is an automated, ordered series of steps that takes a code change from source control to a running system. Source control is the shared history of the code, such as a Git repository. A trigger is the event that starts the pipeline, usually a commit (a saved change) or a merge request. Continuous integration (CI) means every change is merged often and automatically built and tested. Continuous delivery means each passing build is packaged and ready to release with one approval. Continuous deployment goes further and releases automatically with no human approval. A stage is one step of the pipeline, such as build, test, or deploy. An artifact is the packaged output of the build, like a container image or zip file, stored in an artifact repository. A pipeline runner or agent is the machine that executes the stages; Jenkins is a common tool that orchestrates them.

It works because stages run in order and a failure stops everything after it, a quality gate. Bugs are found minutes after they are written, while the change is small and fresh in the author's mind.

Worked example: a developer commits a fix. The trigger fires. Stage one builds the code and produces an artifact tagged with the commit ID. Stage two runs unit tests; one fails, so the pipeline turns red and nothing deploys. The developer fixes the test and commits again. Build passes, tests pass, the same artifact is deployed to a staging environment, smoke tests pass, then a manual approval promotes that exact artifact to production.

Managing a pipeline means keeping its definition as code in source control, storing secrets in a secrets manager rather than in the pipeline file, keeping it fast, and fixing a red build immediately.

A common mistake is rebuilding the code separately for each environment. The production build can then differ from what was tested, so a bug that staging never saw reaches users. Build once, then promote the same artifact.

questions.prompt:
A logistics company runs a CI/CD pipeline for its route-planning API. It practises continuous delivery, meaning every passing build is packaged and ready to release, but a person must approve each production release. Here is one run, traced step by step.

Step 1: An engineer's merge request is merged into the main branch, and the trigger starts the pipeline.
Step 2: The build stage produces a container image tagged r7c2e9 and stores it in the artifact repository.
Step 3: The test stage runs 340 unit tests, and all of them pass.
Step 4: Image r7c2e9 is deployed to the staging environment, and smoke tests pass.
Step 5: ???
Step 6: Production is now running image r7c2e9.

Which action belongs in Step 5?
choices: The pipeline rebuilds the code from the main branch using production settings, creating a fresh image for production.
The engineer copies the production database password into the pipeline file so the release can connect.
After a team lead approves the release, the pipeline promotes the same image r7c2e9 from the artifact repository to production.
The pipeline deploys image r7c2e9 to production automatically, because staging passed and no approval is needed.
questions.why: Continuous delivery requires one human approval, and building once then promoting the exact tested artifact means production runs what staging verified.

questions.prompt: An online ticketing startup sets up its pipeline so that every build that passes all its stages goes straight to production. No person reviews or approves the release. Which practice is this?
choices: Continuous deployment
Continuous integration
Continuous delivery
Source control
questions.why: Continuous deployment releases each passing build automatically with no human approval, while continuous delivery stops for a single approval first.

questions.prompt: A hospital scheduling app has a pipeline with four stages that run in order: build, unit tests, integration tests, and deploy. On one run, the build and unit tests pass, but 2 of the 55 integration tests fail. What happens next?
choices: The pipeline skips the two failed tests and deploys the remaining tested code to production.
The deploy stage runs anyway because the build and unit tests passed, and the failures are logged for later.
The pipeline turns red and the deploy stage does not run, so nothing is released until the problem is fixed and a new commit triggers another run.
The runner automatically rebuilds the code and deploys the new build without testing it.
questions.why: Stages act as a quality gate, so a failure stops every stage after it and nothing deploys.

questions.prompt: At a retail company, a developer adds the payment provider's secret API key directly into the pipeline definition file, which is stored in the team's Git repository. What is the best way to manage this?
choices: Store the key in a secrets manager and have the pipeline fetch it when it runs, keeping it out of the pipeline file.
Move the key into a comment at the bottom of the pipeline file so the runner ignores it.
Remove the pipeline file from source control so that only the developer's laptop holds it.
Leave the key in the file, because keeping the pipeline definition as code in source control is good practice.
questions.why: Good pipeline management keeps secrets in a secrets manager instead of the pipeline file, while the pipeline definition itself stays in source control.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a CI/CD pipeline does from commit to production, why it beats deploying by hand, and name one limit or tradeoff, such as continuous delivery versus continuous deployment.
lessons.modelAnswer: A CI/CD pipeline is automation that starts when someone commits code to source control. It builds the code into an artifact, runs tests, and stops immediately if any stage fails, so broken code never moves forward. CI is the part that integrates and tests every change often; CD packages and delivers it. We build the artifact once and promote that same artifact through staging to production, so what we tested is what we ship. This beats manual deploys because the steps are identical every time, bugs show up minutes after they are written, and releases become small and routine. The tradeoff: continuous deployment pushes every passing change straight to production, which is fast but relies entirely on test quality; continuous delivery adds a human approval, which is safer but slower. Also, a pipeline is only as good as its tests, and a slow pipeline tempts people to bypass it.
rubricPoints: A pipeline is triggered by a change in source control and runs ordered stages such as build, test and deploy.
A failing stage stops the pipeline, acting as a quality gate.
CI means frequent automated build and test; continuous delivery needs an approval, continuous deployment does not.
Build the artifact once and promote the same artifact through environments.
Names a limit, such as dependence on test quality, pipeline speed, or the risk of automatic production releases.

suggested.rationale: Repairing a red CI pipeline makes the learner work directly with stages, triggers and failing gates, which is the core of building and managing a pipeline.

lessons.plain: Integrating systems means connecting separate tools so they pass information to each other automatically, instead of a person copying data from one screen into another. In a cloud team, the monitoring tool, the ticketing system, the chat tool, the code repository and the cloud provider all hold pieces of the picture. When they are wired together, an alert can open a ticket, post a message and attach logs on its own. Think of it like a relay race: each runner hands the baton directly to the next, so nobody has to walk back to the start to fetch it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your monitoring tool spots a full disk at 3 a.m. Today an engineer wakes up, reads the alert, and types a ticket by hand. What would have to be true for the ticket to appear by itself, already filled in?
lessons.teach:
System integration is connecting independent tools so they exchange data and trigger each other without manual steps. Three building blocks do most of the work.

An API (application programming interface) is a defined set of requests a system accepts from other programs. A REST API is the common web style: a program sends an HTTP request such as POST to a URL, usually with a JSON body (a simple text format of named fields), and gets a response. A webhook is the reverse direction: you give a system a URL, and it calls that URL the moment something happens, so the receiver does not have to keep asking (polling). A service account is a non-human identity, with its own token or key, that one system uses to prove who it is to another.

Why it works: each tool keeps doing its own job, but agreed request formats let them cooperate. This is loose coupling, meaning one tool can be replaced as long as the new one speaks the same interface.

Worked example. Step 1: the monitoring tool sees disk usage pass 90 percent. Step 2: it fires a webhook to a small integration service with the host name and value. Step 3: that service calls the ticketing system's REST API with POST, sending a title, severity and host, and authenticates with a service account token. Step 4: the ticketing API replies with a ticket number. Step 5: the service posts that number to the team chat channel. No human touched it, and the ticket is complete and timestamped.

A common mistake is wiring the integration with a personal engineer's login. When that person changes their password or leaves, every automated ticket silently stops. Use a service account with only the permissions it needs, and store its token in a secrets store, not in the script.

In a running system, integrations are also failure points: if the ticketing API is down, alerts can be lost, so integrations need retries, error logging and a check that they are still working.

questions.prompt:
A small online bookshop wants each merge into its main code branch to deploy automatically and announce itself. Here is the flow, with one step missing.

Step 1: A developer merges a change into the main branch of the source repository.
Step 2: The repository immediately fires a webhook to the build server. It sends the branch name and the commit ID, a unique label for that change.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: The hosting platform's API replies with deployment number 4417.
Step 5: The build server posts 'Deployment 4417 started' to the team chat channel.

Which choice correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: The hosting platform fires its own webhook to the build server and asks which commit ID it should deploy next.
The build server sends a POST request to the hosting platform's REST API and signs in with the lead developer's personal username and password.
The build server sends a POST request with a JSON body containing the commit ID to the hosting platform's REST API. It authenticates with a service account token kept in a secrets store.
The build server checks the repository every five minutes to see whether any new commits have arrived since the last check.
questions.why: Step 4 is a reply from the hosting platform's API, so Step 3 must be a request to that REST API, made under a non-human service account identity whose token is held safely in a secrets store.

questions.prompt: At a logistics company, the warehouse system asks the order system every 30 seconds whether any new orders exist. Usually the answer is no, which wastes requests, and new orders can still wait up to 30 seconds. Which integration approach removes this repeated asking?
choices: Give the order system a URL so that it calls the warehouse system as soon as a new order is created. This is a webhook.
Shorten the check interval to every 5 seconds so new orders are spotted sooner.
Create a service account for the warehouse system so its repeated checks are authenticated.
Replace the order system with a different product that has a faster response time.
questions.why: A webhook reverses the direction: the order system calls the receiver the moment an order is created, so the warehouse system no longer has to poll.

questions.prompt: At a clinic, a nightly script calls the storage system's API and emails a backup report. The reports suddenly stopped with no warning on the same day that Marco, the engineer who wrote the script, left the company. What is the most likely cause, and what is the right fix?
choices: The email server is rejecting messages, so the report should be posted to a chat channel instead.
The script signed in with Marco's personal login, which was disabled. It should use a service account with only the permissions it needs, with its token stored in a secrets store.
The storage API was replaced, so the script should be rewritten to poll the storage system instead of calling its API.
The JSON body format changed, so the script needs a new set of named fields.
questions.why: Integrations tied to a person's login silently break when that person leaves. A least-privilege service account whose token is kept in a secrets store does not depend on any one employee.

questions.prompt: A media company's alerting tool creates tickets by sending standard REST API requests to its ticketing product. The company swaps that ticketing product for a new one, and the alerting tool needs no changes at all. Which idea explains this?
choices: Polling, because the alerting tool keeps checking until the new product answers.
Service accounts, because a non-human identity automatically works with any ticketing product.
Webhooks, because the new ticketing product calls the alerting tool whenever a ticket is created.
Loose coupling, because each tool does its own job and talks through an agreed interface, so one tool can be replaced if the new one speaks the same interface.
questions.why: Loose coupling means tools cooperate only through agreed request formats, so one tool can be replaced without changing the others as long as the replacement accepts the same interface.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how connecting our monitoring, ticketing and chat tools would change on-call work, and name one risk or tradeoff the integration introduces.
lessons.modelAnswer: Right now a person reads each alert and retypes it into a ticket, which is slow and error-prone at 3 a.m. If we integrate the tools, the monitoring system sends a webhook the moment a threshold is crossed, a small service calls the ticketing tool's REST API to open a ticket with the host and value filled in, and then posts the ticket number to chat. Each tool keeps its own job; they just agree on request formats, so we could swap one later. The integration should authenticate with a service account that has narrow permissions, with its token kept in a secrets store, not someone's personal login. The tradeoff is that the integration itself becomes something that can fail: if the ticketing API is down or the token expires, alerts could vanish quietly, so we need retries, error logs and a check that it still works.
rubricPoints: Defines integration as tools exchanging data and triggering each other without manual steps.
Distinguishes an API (you call it) from a webhook (it calls you when something happens).
Uses a service account with least privilege and a securely stored token instead of a personal login.
Notes loose coupling lets one tool be replaced if the interface stays the same.
Names a risk such as the integration failing silently and the need for retries, logging or health checks.

suggested.rationale: Fixing how a deploy authenticates to another system without leaking the secret is hands-on practice with the credential wiring that every system integration depends on.

lessons.plain: Kubernetes, Ansible and Jenkins are three popular tools that take repetitive work off a person's hands, each for a different kind of job. Kubernetes runs and looks after containers, which are small packaged apps, keeping the right number running and replacing any that fail. Ansible logs into many servers and puts each one into the setup you described, such as installing software or changing settings. Jenkins waits for new code and then runs the build, test and deploy steps in order. Think of a restaurant: Jenkins is the order ticket system, Ansible is the crew that sets up every kitchen the same way, and Kubernetes is the manager who keeps enough cooks on shift.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team has three chores: keep exactly five copies of a web app running at all times, install the same security patch on 40 servers, and run tests every time someone pushes new code. Which chore would you hand to a tool that watches and repairs things constantly, and which ones only need to run once when asked?
lessons.teach:
