Kubernetes is a container orchestrator, a system that schedules and supervises containers across a group of machines called a cluster. A container is an app packaged with everything it needs to run. Kubernetes groups one or more containers into a pod, its smallest unit. You declare a desired state, for example "three pods of the web app", and Kubernetes keeps comparing that to what is actually running. If a pod crashes, it starts a new one. This constant compare-and-correct loop is why it suits long-running services.

Ansible is a configuration management tool. It is agentless, meaning nothing extra is installed on the target servers; it connects over SSH (a secure remote login). You write a playbook, a YAML text file listing tasks such as "package nginx is installed". Ansible tasks are idempotent: running them twice gives the same result as running once, because each task checks whether the change is already in place. Ansible runs when you start it, then stops.

Jenkins is an automation server used for CI/CD, meaning continuous integration (automatically building and testing every code change) and continuous delivery or deployment (automatically releasing it). A Jenkins pipeline is a sequence of stages, often written in a file called a Jenkinsfile, set off by a trigger such as a code push.

Worked example: a developer pushes a fix. First, Jenkins notices the push and runs the build and test stages. Second, the tests pass, so Jenkins starts a deploy stage. Third, that stage calls Ansible to update settings on the database servers. Fourth, the same stage tells Kubernetes the new container version. Finally, Kubernetes replaces the old pods with new ones while keeping three running.

A common mistake is expecting Ansible or Jenkins to keep an app alive. Each runs once and finishes, so if a container dies at 3 a.m., nothing brings it back. In a running system, that means an outage until a human notices. Self-healing for long-running containers comes from an orchestrator like Kubernetes.

questions.prompt:
A city transit agency runs its trip-planner app on a Kubernetes cluster. Trace the steps and pick the missing one.
Step 1: The team declares a desired state of five pods of the trip-planner.
Step 2: At 2 a.m., one machine in the cluster fails, taking two pods with it, so only three pods are actually running.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: Shortly after, five pods are running again, and no human was involved.
What happens in Step 3?
choices: Jenkins detects the failed machine and reruns the whole pipeline to redeploy the trip-planner from scratch.
Ansible reruns its playbook on its own, because idempotent tasks repeat automatically when servers fail.
Kubernetes compares the desired five pods with the three actually running and starts two new pods.
Kubernetes waits for the next code push to trigger a restart, then recreates the two missing pods.
questions.why: Kubernetes keeps comparing the declared desired state with what is actually running and corrects any gap by starting replacement pods, which is its self-healing loop.

questions.prompt: An admin at a regional hospital writes an Ansible playbook with the task "the user account backupsvc exists" and runs it against 40 servers. All 40 now have the account. The next morning she runs the exact same playbook again by mistake. What happens on those 40 servers?
choices: The run fails on all 40 servers, because Ansible refuses to touch a server it has already configured.
Ansible first installs its agent on the servers, then deletes and recreates the account to reset it.
Each task checks that the account already exists and makes no further change, so the result is the same as one run.
Ansible creates a second backupsvc account on each server, because every run repeats every task.
questions.why: Ansible tasks are idempotent: each one checks whether the change is already in place, so running twice gives the same result as running once.

questions.prompt: A small online retailer wants every change a developer pushes to its checkout code to be built and tested automatically, and released if the tests pass. Which tool from this objective fits that job best?
choices: A container, because it packages the checkout app with everything it needs to run.
Jenkins, because it runs a CI/CD pipeline of stages that is set off by a trigger such as a code push.
Kubernetes, because it keeps comparing the desired number of pods with the number actually running.
Ansible, because it connects over SSH without installing anything on the target servers.
questions.why: Jenkins is an automation server for CI/CD, building, testing and releasing code changes through pipeline stages triggered by events such as a push.

questions.prompt: An engineering team at a logistics firm uses a nightly Jenkins job at 1 a.m. that calls an Ansible playbook to start its tracking app's container on a server. They do not use Kubernetes. At 4 a.m., the container crashes. What is the most likely result?
choices: Ansible notices the crash over SSH and restarts the container, because its tasks are idempotent.
The container restarts itself, because a container includes everything it needs to run.
The app stays down until a human notices, because Jenkins and Ansible each run once and finish.
Jenkins restarts the container right away, because a CI/CD pipeline supervises running apps.
questions.why: Jenkins and Ansible run when started and then stop, so nothing watches the container afterwards; self-healing for long-running containers comes from an orchestrator like Kubernetes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Kubernetes, Ansible and Jenkins each do, how they can work together in one release, and one limit of each tool that means you would not use it for the others' job.
lessons.modelAnswer: They automate different layers. Jenkins is an automation server for CI/CD: a code push triggers a pipeline of stages that build, test and deploy. Ansible is agentless configuration management: it connects over SSH and applies a YAML playbook so servers end up in a described state, and its tasks are idempotent, so rerunning is safe. Kubernetes orchestrates containers: you declare a desired state like three pods, and it keeps correcting reality to match, restarting failed pods. In one release, Jenkins tests the change, calls Ansible to configure servers, then updates the container version in Kubernetes. Limits: Jenkins and Ansible run once and stop, so neither keeps an app alive afterwards. Kubernetes only manages containers in its cluster, so it will not configure a plain server outside it, and it does not decide when code is ready to ship.
rubricPoints: Kubernetes orchestrates containers and continuously enforces a declared desired state, self-healing failed pods.
Ansible is agentless configuration management using SSH and YAML playbooks with idempotent tasks.
Jenkins is a CI/CD automation server that runs pipeline stages when triggered, such as by a code push.
The tools can chain together in one release, with Jenkins calling the others.
Names a real limit, such as Ansible and Jenkins running once and not keeping services alive.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing the right tool for a described task, so reasoning through tool-selection scenarios adds the most, and no current mission or planned engine has the learner operate Kubernetes, Ansible or Jenkins directly.

lessons.plain: An event-driven architecture is a way of building software where parts of a system react to things that happen, instead of constantly asking each other for updates. An event is a short message saying something occurred, like 'a file was uploaded' or 'an order was paid.' One part announces the event, and any part that cares reacts to it. Think of a doorbell: you do not stand at the window checking for visitors every minute. The bell rings, and you respond. In the cloud, this lets small pieces work independently, scale on their own, and run only when there is actual work to do.
lessons.guessPrompt: A photo-sharing app must make a small thumbnail every time someone uploads a picture. Would you rather have a program check the storage every ten seconds for new photos, or have the upload itself announce 'new photo' so a thumbnail maker can respond? What might go wrong with each choice?
lessons.teach:
An event-driven architecture is a design where components communicate by producing and reacting to events. An event is a record that something happened, such as a new file or a completed payment. A producer is the component that emits the event. A consumer is a component that receives the event and does work in response. Between them sits a broker, a managed service that holds and delivers events; it might be a queue (each message goes to one consumer) or a publish/subscribe topic, often called pub/sub (each message is copied to every subscriber). A common consumer is a serverless function, code the cloud provider runs only when triggered, so you pay per run rather than for an idle server.

This works because of loose coupling: the producer does not know or wait for its consumers. You can add a new consumer without changing the producer, and the broker absorbs traffic spikes by buffering events until consumers catch up. Work happens asynchronously, meaning the producer moves on immediately.

Worked example: a user uploads cat.jpg to object storage. Step one, the storage service emits an 'object created' event. Step two, the event lands on a pub/sub topic. Step three, two subscribers each receive a copy: a function that builds a thumbnail, and a function that writes an audit log entry. Step four, each function finishes and acknowledges the event, so the broker removes it. If the thumbnail function crashes, the broker redelivers the event later.

A common mistake is assuming each event arrives exactly once and in order. Most brokers guarantee at-least-once delivery, so duplicates happen. Consumers must be idempotent, meaning processing the same event twice gives the same result as processing it once. In a running system, a non-idempotent payment handler can charge a customer twice, and a message that always fails, called a poison message, can be retried forever unless it is moved aside to a dead-letter queue, a holding area for events that keep failing.

questions.prompt: A logistics company uses an event-driven design to handle delivered parcels. Step one: a driver marks parcel P-4471 as delivered, and the tracking service emits a 'parcel delivered' event. Step two: the event lands on a publish/subscribe (pub/sub) topic with three subscribers: a function that texts the customer, a function that adds a 40-cent delivery fee to the merchant's bill, and a function that updates a dashboard. Step three: the billing function adds the fee but crashes before it acknowledges the event, so the broker later delivers the same event to it again. Step four: ______. Which choice correctly completes step four?
choices: The tracking service notices the crash and resends the event directly to the billing function, then waits for it to finish.
The broker removes the event from all three subscribers, because one subscriber failed to acknowledge it.
The billing function adds a second 40-cent fee, because the broker only redelivers events that were never processed.
The billing function checks whether parcel P-4471 has already been billed, skips the duplicate charge, and acknowledges the event.
questions.why: Brokers deliver at least once, so the billing consumer must be idempotent: processing the same event twice must give the same result as processing it once, which means one fee, not two.

questions.prompt: A video-hosting startup runs five identical worker instances that convert uploaded videos to smaller formats. Each uploaded video should be converted by exactly one worker, not by all five. Which type of broker fits this need?
choices: A queue, where each message goes to one consumer
No broker; the upload service should call all five workers directly and wait for them
A dead-letter queue, where all new uploads are held
A pub/sub topic, where each message is copied to every subscriber
questions.why: A queue hands each message to a single consumer, so the five workers share the load without converting the same video several times.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company's checkout service already publishes a 'ticket sold' event to a pub/sub topic. The security team wants to add a fraud-check function that reacts to every sale. Why can they do this without changing or redeploying the checkout service?
choices: Because the broker guarantees each event is delivered exactly once and in order
Because of loose coupling: the producer does not know about its consumers, so a new subscriber can simply be added to the topic
Because the checkout service waits for each consumer to reply before it continues
Because serverless functions are charged per run, so adding one costs nothing
questions.why: In an event-driven architecture the producer only emits events to the broker and does not know or wait for consumers, so new consumers can subscribe without touching the producer.

questions.prompt: A payroll application receives a 'timesheet submitted' event that contains corrupted data. The consumer function crashes every time it reads this event, and the broker has now redelivered it more than 3,000 times. What is the right way to handle this kind of event?
choices: Turn off at-least-once delivery so the broker never retries any event
After a set number of failed attempts, move the event to a dead-letter queue, a holding area for events that keep failing
Have the producer stop emitting timesheet events until the consumer is rewritten
Switch the topic to a queue so only one consumer has to fail
questions.why: An event that always fails is a poison message, and moving it aside to a dead-letter queue stops it from being retried forever while other events keep flowing.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, what an event-driven architecture is and why we might use one for a cloud app. Include at least one limit or tradeoff they need to design around.
lessons.modelAnswer: In an event-driven design, components don't call each other directly. A producer announces that something happened, like 'order paid,' by sending an event to a broker such as a queue or pub/sub topic. Consumers, often serverless functions, pick up those events and do their work. The big win is loose coupling: the producer doesn't wait for or even know about the consumers, so we can add new reactions without touching it, and the broker buffers bursts so each piece scales on its own. We also only pay for functions when events actually arrive. The tradeoff is that things become asynchronous and harder to trace end to end. Brokers usually deliver at least once, so duplicates and out-of-order events happen. Handlers must be idempotent, and we need a dead-letter queue so a message that always fails doesn't block or loop forever.
rubricPoints: Defines an event and the producer, broker, and consumer roles.
Explains loose coupling and asynchronous processing as the main benefit.
Mentions buffering or independent scaling, or paying only when events occur.
Names at-least-once delivery or ordering as a limit.
Says consumers must be idempotent or that failing messages need a dead-letter queue.

suggested.rationale: Writing an idempotent event handler makes the learner confront at-least-once delivery, the core practical consequence of event-driven design.

scenarios.title: Hybrid plan for a growing kitchen-supply distributor
scenarios.scenario:
Copperleaf Kitchen Supply is a fictional regional company that sells cooking equipment to restaurants. It runs everything today on three physical servers in a closet at its head office. You have joined as a junior cloud engineer, and your manager wants a written recommendation by Friday.

Here is what you learn. The online ordering website is quiet most of the year, but traffic jumps about five times higher for six weeks before the winter holidays. The site currently crashes during that rush. The payroll and HR system holds employee records, and a signed agreement with the staff union says those records must stay on hardware the company owns, in its own building. A product database (an organized store of records the website reads and writes, such as items, prices and stock counts) needs to be reachable by the website at all times. Every night at 1 a.m. a reporting job runs for about two hours and then stops. Finance has also noticed that two test virtual machines (software-based computers that run on shared physical hardware) were left running all last quarter at full size even though they were barely used.

Some terms you will need. A deployment model describes where computing resources live and who controls them. Public cloud means renting resources from a provider and sharing its hardware with other customers. Private cloud means cloud-style resources dedicated to one organization, often in its own building. Hybrid cloud joins public and private together so they work as one system. Multi-cloud means using more than one public cloud provider. A virtual network is a private, software-defined network inside a cloud provider, which you divide into subnets (smaller address ranges you can treat differently, for example one reachable from the internet and one not). A VPN, or virtual private network, is an encrypted tunnel that carries traffic safely across the public internet; a site-to-site VPN links a whole office network to a whole cloud network. A container is a lightweight package holding an application and everything it needs to run, so it behaves the same on any host. Orchestration is software, such as Kubernetes, that starts, stops, restarts and scales many containers automatically. Rightsizing means changing a resource to the size it actually needs. Reserved capacity is a discount for promising to use a resource for a long period, and spot capacity is spare provider capacity sold cheaply that can be taken back at short notice.

Answer the following.
1. Recommend one deployment model for Copperleaf and explain which workloads go where, using the facts above.
2. Describe how the head office should connect to the cloud, and how the cloud virtual network should be laid out for the website and the product database.
3. Explain how containers and orchestration would stop the website from crashing during the holiday rush.
4. Recommend specific cost moves for the test virtual machines, the nightly reporting job, the always-on product database, and for tracking spending going forward.
subParts: Design the network connection and layout
Use containers and orchestration for the rush
modelAnswer: Hybrid cloud. The payroll and HR system must stay on company-owned hardware in the company's building because of the union agreement, so it stays on-premises (or in a private cloud at head office). The ordering website, which has a large seasonal spike, belongs in the public cloud, where capacity can be added for the six-week rush and removed afterward instead of buying hardware that sits idle most of the year. The product database and nightly reporting job also fit the public cloud alongside the website. Public-only is wrong because it breaks the payroll requirement; private-only is wrong because it cannot absorb the spike without buying extra hardware; multi-cloud adds a second provider and extra complexity without solving any stated problem.

Use a site-to-site VPN from the head office network to the cloud virtual network, so traffic between payroll at the office and cloud systems travels through an encrypted tunnel across the internet rather than in the open. Inside the virtual network, create at least two subnets: a public-facing subnet for the website, which customers must reach from the internet, and a private subnet for the product database with no direct internet access, allowing only the website (and the office over the VPN, if needed) to reach it. This keeps the database reachable by the website at all times while reducing its exposure to attackers.

Package the website as a container so every copy is identical and starts quickly. An orchestrator such as Kubernetes then runs several copies spread across hosts and automatically adds more copies as traffic rises during the holiday rush, then removes them when traffic falls. If a copy fails, the orchestrator restarts or replaces it, so one failure does not take the site down. The result is that capacity follows demand, avoiding the crashes, without paying for peak capacity all year. A common mistake is running a single container with no orchestration, which gives none of the automatic scaling or self-healing.

Test virtual machines: rightsize them to a smaller size that matches their low use, and shut them down or schedule them off when not in use, since leaving them at full size all quarter wasted money. Nightly reporting job: run it on capacity that exists only during its two-hour window, such as spot capacity or a scheduled resource that starts at 1 a.m. and stops afterward, because the job is short and can be rerun if interrupted. Always-on product database: buy reserved capacity, because it runs constantly and a long-term commitment gives a discount over paying by the hour. Tracking spending: label (tag) every resource with its owner and purpose, review the billing and usage reports regularly, and set budget alerts so finance is warned before costs exceed the plan instead of discovering waste at quarter end.

scenarios.title: Moving Larkspur Veterinary Supply's Order System to the Cloud
scenarios.scenario:
Larkspur Veterinary Supply is a fictional company that sells medical supplies to animal clinics. Its order system runs on two aging physical servers in a back office: one runs the web application that clinics use to place orders, and the other runs the database (the organized store of customer, product, and order records). The hardware support contract ends in three months, so the IT manager, Priya, has asked you to help move this workload (the application plus the data and servers it needs) to a public cloud provider.

Priya has shared a few facts. Clinics place most orders between 7 a.m. and 10 a.m. on weekdays. The web server also sends nightly files to a shipping partner over a fixed connection, and a separate reporting tool in the office reads directly from the database. The business says it can tolerate at most four hours of downtime (time when the system is unavailable) during the move, and it cannot lose more than 15 minutes of order data if something goes wrong. Last year a teammate built a test server by clicking through the cloud provider's web console (its point-and-click management website), and nobody can now say exactly how it was configured.

Priya wants a plan, not a rushed copy. Complete the following tasks.

1. Before choosing any cloud resources, list the requirements you would gather about the current system, and explain why each one matters for the migration.
2. Recommend a migration approach for the first move, and describe a cutover plan (the steps for switching users from the old system to the new one) that respects the four-hour downtime limit and the 15-minute data-loss limit, including how you would back out if it fails.
3. Explain why the new environment should be built with infrastructure as code (IaC) rather than by clicking through the console, using last year's test server as your example.
4. Describe how you would provision (create and set up) and configure the cloud resources so they fit the workload, cost a sensible amount, and are reasonably secure.
modelAnswer: Gather a performance baseline, meaning measurements of normal and peak use over a few weeks: CPU (processor) load, memory, storage size and growth, disk speed, and network traffic, especially during the 7 to 10 a.m. weekday peak. This matters because cloud servers are chosen by size, and guessing leads to either slow orders at peak or paying for unused capacity. Map dependencies, meaning other systems this workload talks to: the nightly file transfer to the shipping partner and the office reporting tool that reads the database. If these are missed, they break after the move even though the main app works. Record the business limits: the four-hour downtime limit is the recovery time objective (RTO, the longest acceptable outage) and the 15-minute data-loss limit is the recovery point objective (RPO, the largest acceptable gap in lost data). These decide how the data is copied and when the cutover happens. Also note operating system and software versions, licensing, and any rules about where customer data may be stored, because these can limit which cloud services can be used. A common mistake is measuring only on a quiet day, which undersizes the system and makes it slow when clinics are busiest.

For the first move, a rehost approach (often called lift-and-shift, moving the servers largely as they are onto cloud virtual machines, which are software-based servers) is a sound choice because the hardware deadline is close and it changes the least. A reasonable alternative is to replatform only the database, moving it to a managed database service (one where the provider handles patching and backups), if the team is comfortable with that. Cutover plan: build and test the cloud environment first; copy the bulk data ahead of time; then keep the cloud database continuously synchronized with the old one (ongoing replication) so the gap stays under 15 minutes. Schedule the cutover outside the 7 to 10 a.m. peak, for example on a weekend night. During the window: stop new orders on the old system, let the final changes sync, check that record counts match, switch the address users connect to so it points at the cloud system, and test placing an order, the shipping file transfer, and the reporting tool. Rollback: keep the old servers untouched and ready, set a decision point well inside the four hours, and if tests fail, point users back to the old system. The common mistake is shutting down or wiping the old servers too soon, leaving no way back.

Infrastructure as code means describing servers, networks, and settings in text files that a tool reads to build the environment automatically. The files act as an exact, repeatable recipe. The test server built by clicking in the console shows the problem: nobody knows its exact settings, so it cannot be rebuilt identically, reviewed, or audited. With IaC, the files are kept in version control (a system that records every change, who made it, and why), so the team can see history and undo mistakes. The same files can build matching test and production environments, so what was tested is what goes live. Most IaC tools are declarative (you state the desired end result, not every step) and idempotent (running them again produces the same result instead of creating duplicates). They also help detect configuration drift, which is when someone changes a live system by hand so it no longer matches the files. A common mistake is using IaC to build but then fixing problems by hand in the console, which reintroduces drift and an unknown setup.

Right-size the resources: choose virtual machine sizes and storage based on the baseline from task 1, with some headroom for the morning peak, rather than copying the old hardware specs or picking the largest option. Consider automatic scaling (adding capacity when load rises and removing it when it falls) for the web tier if the peak is sharp. Place the servers in a virtual network (a private, isolated network inside the cloud), with the web server reachable by clinics and the database in a private section that only the web server and reporting tool can reach. Use security groups or firewall rules (lists of allowed traffic) that open only the needed ports, and give people and services only the permissions they need (least privilege). Turn on encryption for stored data, set up automated backups that meet the 15-minute RPO, and enable monitoring and alerts. Apply tags (labels such as owner, application, and environment) to every resource so costs and ownership are easy to track. Define all of this in the IaC files from task 3 so it is consistent. A common mistake is leaving the database open to the internet or oversizing everything, which creates a security risk or an unnecessarily large bill.

scenarios.title: Securing the Checkout at Tallowmere Outfitters
scenarios.scenario:
Tallowmere Outfitters is a small fictional online shop that sells camping gear. Its website runs in a public cloud. A public cloud is computing power and storage rented from a provider over the internet. Customers pay by credit card on the site. You have just joined as a junior cloud engineer, and your manager asks you to review security before the busy holiday season. You find four problems.

First, the access problem. Identity and access management (IAM) is the system that decides who, or what, can do which actions on which cloud resources. All five developers sign in with one shared administrator account. An administrator account can do anything. The account has no multi-factor authentication (MFA), which is a sign-in check that asks for a second proof, such as a code from a phone app, on top of the password. The checkout application also reaches the database using an access key. An access key is a long-lived secret, like a permanent password for a program. This key is typed directly into the application's source code and has full administrator rights. The guiding rule for good IAM is least privilege: give each person or program only the permissions its job needs, and nothing more.

Second, the container problem. A container is a lightweight package that holds an application plus everything it needs to run, built from a starting template called a base image. The checkout container runs as root. Root is the all-powerful user inside a system. Its base image is two years old. A scan lists several CVEs in it. A CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures entry) is a publicly numbered, known security flaw. The container can also write to its whole file system, even though the app only needs to write log files.

Third, the compliance problem. Compliance means proving that you follow a set of security rules that someone outside your company has defined. The finance lead has heard of three standards and asks which one is required for taking card payments. PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) is a set of rules from the card brands. Any business that stores, processes, or sends cardholder data must follow it. SOC 2 (System and Organization Controls 2) is a report written by an independent auditor. It describes how well a service company protects its customers' data. Companies usually get it because their business customers ask for it. ISO 27001 is an international standard for running an information security management system (ISMS). An ISMS is the organized set of policies, risk reviews, and processes a company uses to manage security. A company can choose to be certified against it.

Fourth, the storage problem. Product photos and nightly order exports are kept in an object storage bucket. An object storage bucket is a cloud container for files that are reached over the internet. The bucket is set to public, so anyone with the link can read it. The order exports include customer names, addresses, and the last four digits of card numbers. Nobody noticed, because no tool regularly checks the cloud settings.

Your tasks:
1. Fix the IAM problems. Name the specific changes for the developers and for the checkout application, and explain why each change reduces risk.
2. Harden the checkout container. Name at least three specific changes and the risk each one addresses.
3. Tell the finance lead which standard is required for taking card payments. Explain why that one is required, and how the other two differ.
4. Fix the storage exposure, and name one control that would catch this kind of mistake in future.
subParts: IAM fixes for people and the app
modelAnswer: For the developers: remove the shared administrator account from daily use. Give each developer an individual account so every action can be traced to one person. Group developers and give the group only the permissions their work needs, which is least privilege. Turn on MFA for every account, so a stolen password alone is not enough to sign in. Keep any remaining administrator access for a small number of people, also protected by MFA. For the checkout application: remove the access key from the source code, because anyone who can read the code, or a leaked copy of it, gets the secret. Replace it with a role. A role is an identity the application takes on that hands it short-lived, automatically rotated credentials. If you must keep a key, store it in a secrets manager and rotate it. Limit the app's permissions to only the database actions it needs, not full administrator rights. Why it works: individual accounts give accountability, MFA blocks stolen-password attacks, and least privilege plus short-lived credentials shrink what an attacker can do if something leaks. Common mistake: adding MFA but leaving the shared account and the full-admin key in place.

At least three of the following, each tied to its risk. 1. Run the app as a non-root user. If an attacker breaks into the app, they do not get all-powerful rights inside the container, which makes it harder to escape or tamper with it. 2. Rebuild from an up-to-date, minimal base image that has the CVE fixes. This removes the known flaws, and including fewer packages leaves fewer things to attack. 3. Scan images for CVEs automatically before they are deployed, and block images with serious findings. This stops known flaws from reaching production again. 4. Make the container's file system read-only, with one writable location only for logs. An attacker then cannot drop tools or change the app's files. Removing unneeded privileges and capabilities is also acceptable. Consequence for a running system: an unhardened container running as root with known CVEs gives an attacker an easy foothold, close to the payment flow.

PCI DSS is required. The shop takes card payments, and PCI DSS applies to any business that stores, processes, or sends cardholder data. The card brands set it, so it is not optional. SOC 2 is different: it is an independent auditor's report on how a service company protects its customers' data. It is usually requested by business customers and is not the rule for accepting cards. ISO 27001 is also different: it is a voluntary certification for running an organized security management system (an ISMS). Both can be valuable, but neither replaces PCI DSS for card payments. Common mistake: picking whichever standard sounds most general or most well known, instead of the one that matches the data and the risk.

Immediately make the bucket private by turning off public access, and block public access at the account level if the provider allows it. Then grant read access only to the identities that need it, following least privilege. If photos must be public, move them to a separate bucket, and keep the order exports private. Make sure the exports are encrypted at rest, meaning stored in scrambled form. Also review whether full exports with customer data are needed at all, and treat the exposure as a possible incident to investigate. Detection control: use automated configuration scanning, such as a cloud security posture management tool or regular vulnerability and configuration scans. These continuously check settings like public buckets against a policy and raise alerts. Why: the problem went unnoticed because nothing checked the settings, and an automated check would flag a public bucket as soon as it appeared.

scenarios.title: Holiday Rush at Larkspur Kitchen Supply
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined the operations team at Larkspur Kitchen Supply, a fictional online store that sells baking equipment. Its ordering website runs in a public cloud. Customer traffic reaches a load balancer, which is a service that spreads incoming requests across several servers. Behind it sit three identical virtual machines (software-defined servers rented from the cloud provider) running the web application, plus one managed database, which is a database the provider runs and maintains for you.

The site is already live, and your manager says deployment was only the beginning. Four problems are waiting.

First, last December traffic tripled during the holiday sale. The three servers hit 95% CPU (processor) use and customers saw timeouts. Someone suggested replacing each server with a bigger one. That is called vertical scaling, which means adding power to a single machine. Another option is horizontal scaling, which means adding more machines of the same size. Horizontal scaling can be done by autoscaling, a feature that adds or removes servers automatically based on a measured value.

Second, a security patch for the web application's operating system must be applied this week. Last time the team patched all three servers at once, the site went down for 40 minutes.

Third, the database is backed up once a night at 1:00 a.m. The business has set two targets. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the most data, measured in time, the business can afford to lose, and it is set at 1 hour. The recovery time objective (RTO) is the longest the site may be down while being restored, and it is set at 4 hours. The nightly backups are stored in the same region (the same geographic group of data centers) as the database, and nobody has ever tried restoring one.

Fourth, the monitoring dashboard shows that page response time has risen from a normal 300 milliseconds to 2.5 seconds over the past week. Server CPU averages a comfortable 40%, but the database's count of active connections sits at its maximum limit for much of the day. There are no alerts set up, so the team only noticed when customers complained.

Your tasks:
1. Recommend a scaling approach for the web servers before the next holiday sale. Say whether it should be vertical or horizontal, and describe how autoscaling should be configured.
2. Describe a safer way to apply this week's patch to the web servers without taking the site offline, including what to do if the patch causes problems.
3. Explain whether the current backup setup meets the RPO and RTO, and recommend changes.
4. Interpret the monitoring data to identify the likely bottleneck, and describe how the team should monitor so that problems are caught before customers notice.
modelAnswer:
Use horizontal scaling with autoscaling. The web servers are identical and sit behind a load balancer, so adding more of them spreads the load. It also removes the single point of failure that one large server would create. Vertical scaling usually needs a restart to resize the machine, and it hits a ceiling at the largest available size.

Configure an autoscaling group with a minimum of 3 servers to keep today's baseline capacity and redundancy. Set a maximum of, for example, 10 servers to cap cost. Use a scale-out rule such as adding a server when average CPU stays above 70% for 5 minutes, and a scale-in rule such as removing one when CPU stays below 30% for 10 to 15 minutes. Add a cooldown period so new servers have time to start before another scaling decision is made. This prevents rapid flapping up and down.

The new servers must be built from the same image or template so they are identical, and they must register with the load balancer automatically. Because the sale date is known, the team could also schedule extra capacity ahead of it. A strong answer also notes that more web servers increase database load, which links to task 4.

Use a rolling update. Take one server out of the load balancer, a step often called draining it, so it stops receiving new requests. Patch and restart that server, run a health check, and return it to the pool. Then repeat with the next server. The other two servers keep serving customers the whole time, so there is no outage.

An acceptable alternative is a blue-green approach. Patched servers are built alongside the old ones, and traffic is switched over once they pass checks.

Before starting, test the patch in a non-production (staging) environment. Take snapshots or keep the previous image so the change can be reversed. Schedule the work in a low-traffic maintenance window. Have a rollback plan: if the first patched server fails its health check or shows errors, stop the rollout and restore that server from its snapshot or previous image, leaving the unpatched servers serving traffic. Patching all servers at once, as happened last time, is the mistake that caused the 40-minute outage.

It does not meet the RPO. With only one backup a night, a failure at 11:59 p.m. would lose almost 23 hours of orders, far more than the 1-hour limit.

The RTO cannot be confirmed either, because no restore has ever been tested, so nobody knows whether recovery takes 1 hour or 10. Storing the only backups in the same region also means a regional outage could destroy both the database and its backups.

Recommendations: keep the nightly full backup, but add more frequent protection, such as hourly incremental backups or snapshots, or continuous transaction log backups that allow point-in-time recovery. Any of these keeps possible data loss under 1 hour. Copy backups to a second region, or other off-site storage, so a single disaster cannot remove them. Set a retention period that defines how long backups are kept. Most important, schedule regular test restores into a separate environment and time them, to prove recovery fits within 4 hours and that the restored data is complete and usable. A backup that has never been restored cannot be trusted.

CPU at 40% shows the web servers are not the bottleneck, so adding servers would not fix this slowdown. The database connection count sitting at its maximum is the likely cause. New requests must wait for a free connection, which explains why response time rose from 300 ms to 2.5 seconds. Possible fixes include raising the connection limit or the database size, using connection pooling (letting the application reuse a set of open connections instead of opening new ones), finding and tuning slow queries, or adding read replicas (copies of the database that handle read-only requests) to share the load.

For monitoring, record a baseline, which is the normal range for key metrics such as response time, error rate, CPU, memory, and database connections. Then set alert thresholds against that baseline. Examples: alert when response time exceeds about 1 second for 5 minutes, or when database connections pass 80% of the limit. Send alerts to the on-call team so problems are found before customers report them. Review trends on dashboards and in logs over time to spot gradual growth and plan capacity ahead, rather than reacting only to failures.

scenarios.title: Brightlane Bakeries: A Bad Launch Morning
scenarios.scenario:
Brightlane Bakeries, a fictional regional bakery chain, moved its online ordering app to a public cloud last night. You are the junior cloud engineer on call. The app runs on two web servers (virtual machines, meaning software-based computers rented from the cloud provider) inside a virtual network, which is a private, isolated network the company controls inside the provider's data centre. The web servers sit in one subnet, meaning a smaller slice of that network's address range, and the database server sits in a second subnet. Each server is protected by a security group, which is a virtual firewall attached to the server that only allows traffic matching its rules.

At 7:00 a.m. four problems are reported.

First, the web servers start, but every page shows "cannot connect to database." You check the database server's security group. Its only inbound rule allows TCP port 5432 from the source 10.0.1.0/24. A port is a numbered door on a server that a specific service listens on; this database listens on port 5432. A source written like 10.0.1.0/24 is a range of addresses, here 10.0.1.0 to 10.0.1.255. The web servers' addresses are 10.0.2.15 and 10.0.2.16. From a web server, a test connection to the database on port 5432 times out, but the database itself is running and reports it is healthy.

Second, the billing team sees 40 large virtual machines that nobody at Brightlane requested, all created at 3:12 a.m. in a region the company never uses. The provider's audit log, which is a record of every action taken in the account and which identity performed it, shows they were created with an access key belonging to a deployment account called deploy-bot. An access key is a long-lived secret, like a password for software, that lets a program act in the cloud account. A developer admits he pasted that key into a configuration file and pushed it to a public code repository (an online store of source code that anyone can read) yesterday afternoon. deploy-bot has full administrator permissions.

Third, customers who do reach the login page get "token expired" immediately after signing in. The login system issues tokens, which are short-lived digital passes stamped with a creation time and an expiry time. The clock on web server 1 reads 7:14 a.m. while the correct time is 7:02 a.m. Its time service is configured to use NTP, the Network Time Protocol, which keeps a machine's clock correct by regularly asking a time server over UDP port 123. UDP is a quick, connectionless way of sending network messages. The time service logs show "no response from time server" since the move. Last week, someone added an outbound rule to the web servers' security group allowing only TCP ports 443 and 5432 out.

Fourth, some customers typing order.brightlane.example still land on the old on-premises server, which was shut down this morning. The DNS A record for that name was changed to the new cloud address at 6:30 a.m. DNS, the Domain Name System, is the internet's directory that turns names into IP addresses, and an A record is the entry that maps a name to an IPv4 address. The record's TTL, or time to live, which tells other systems how long they may keep a remembered copy of the answer, was 86,400 seconds.

Your tasks:
1. Identify why the web servers cannot reach the database and state the exact fix.
2. List, in order, the steps you would take to contain and recover from the leaked deploy-bot access key, and name one change that limits damage next time.
3. Explain why logins fail with "token expired" and how to fix the root cause rather than the symptom.
4. Explain why some customers still reach the old server, what you can and cannot do about it now, and what should have been done before the cutover.
modelAnswer: The database security group only allows port 5432 from 10.0.1.0/24 (10.0.1.0 to 10.0.1.255), but the web servers live in 10.0.2.0/24 at 10.0.2.15 and 10.0.2.16, so their traffic matches no rule and is silently dropped. That is why the test times out rather than being refused, and why the database looks healthy: the service is fine, the path to it is blocked. Fix: change the inbound rule source to 10.0.2.0/24 (or, more tightly, the two web server addresses or the web servers' security group) on TCP port 5432. Do not open the port to 0.0.0.0/0 (everyone) as a shortcut; that would expose the database to the internet. Re-test the connection from a web server to confirm.

Order matters. 1) Contain: immediately deactivate or delete the deploy-bot access key so the attacker loses access; deleting the file from the repository is not enough because the key was already public and may be copied. 2) Investigate: use the audit log to list everything that key did since it was pushed, including the 40 machines, any new users, keys, roles or permission changes the attacker created (a sign of privilege escalation, meaning gaining more power than intended, or of a hidden way back in). 3) Eradicate: terminate the unauthorised machines, remove any accounts, keys or permissions the attacker added, and check the unused region. 4) Recover: issue a new key (rotation, meaning replacing the secret) stored in a secrets manager or the pipeline's protected variables, update the deployment pipeline, and remove the old key from the repository's history. 5) Report to security and billing (the provider may need to know about fraudulent charges) and record lessons learned. Damage limiter for next time: give deploy-bot least privilege, only the permissions it needs in the regions it uses, instead of administrator rights; scanning commits for secrets before they are pushed and preferring short-lived credentials are also valid answers.

Web server 1's clock is 12 minutes fast. Tokens are stamped with its wrong time, or the server compares a correctly stamped token against its fast clock, so a token with a short lifetime already looks expired. The clock drifted because NTP cannot reach its time server: the new outbound rule only allows TCP 443 and 5432, but NTP uses UDP port 123, so its requests are dropped, matching the "no response from time server" log. Root-cause fix: add an outbound rule allowing UDP 123 to the approved time server (or use the provider's internal time service if one is offered), then confirm the time service syncs and the clock corrects. Manually setting the clock or lengthening token lifetimes only hides the symptom; the clock would drift again, and longer tokens weaken security.

The A record was changed correctly, but its old TTL was 86,400 seconds, which is 24 hours. Resolvers (the DNS servers that look up names on customers' behalf) and devices that fetched the old answer before 6:30 a.m. may keep using the old IP for up to a day, so those customers reach the shut-down server. Now you cannot force other organisations' resolvers to forget the cached answer; the stale copies will expire on their own. What you can do: leave the old server running, or put a redirect at the old address, until 24 hours after the change, and tell affected users to clear local DNS caches. Lowering the TTL now does not help copies already cached with the long TTL. Before the cutover, the TTL should have been lowered (for example to 300 seconds) at least one full old TTL period ahead, so caches would refresh within minutes at switchover, then raised again after the move was stable.

scenarios.title: Ending the Copy-and-Paste Deployments at Larkspur Outfitters
scenarios.scenario:
Larkspur Outfitters is a fictional online shop that sells hiking gear. You have just joined its small cloud operations team. Here is how work gets done today.

The web store runs on 14 virtual machines (software computers rented from a cloud provider). When a setting changes, such as the address of the payment service, a senior engineer named Dana logs in to each machine one at a time and edits a configuration file (a text file that tells the program how to behave). Last month she missed two machines, and for a day some customers saw checkout errors while others did not.

The developers keep the store's code in folders on their own laptops and email zip files to each other. Nobody can say which version is running in production (the live system customers use). When a release is ready, a developer copies files to the servers by hand. Tests, meaning small programs that check the code still works, are run only when someone remembers.

Customers can also upload photos of their trips. A script on Dana's laptop runs every night to shrink those photos into thumbnails (small preview images). If her laptop is off, no thumbnails appear, and on busy days customers wait up to 24 hours.

Your manager asks you to propose fixes using DevOps practices. DevOps is a way of working where the people who build software and the people who run it share tools and automate repeated steps instead of doing them by hand. Answer the following.

1. Explain how the team should use source control to manage both the store's code and its configuration files. Name the tool type, and describe how a developer would safely propose a change.

2. Describe a CI/CD pipeline for the web store using Jenkins. Say what CI and CD each mean, and list the stages the pipeline should run, in order, when a change is merged.

3. Dana's manual edits to 14 machines caused the checkout outage. Explain how Ansible would replace that work, and what the word idempotent means and why it matters here.

4. Redesign the thumbnail job as an event-driven process. Explain what an event is, what would trigger the work, and why this is better than the nightly laptop script.
subParts: Source control for code and configuration
modelAnswer: Use a source control system, which is a tool that records every change to a set of files, who made it and when, and lets you go back to any earlier version. Git is the common example. Put the store's code and the configuration files in one shared repository, a central project store that everyone works from, hosted on a shared server rather than on laptops. To propose a change, a developer creates a branch, which is a separate line of work copied from the main version so changes do not disturb it. They commit (save a recorded snapshot of) their edits on that branch, then open a pull request, a formal request asking teammates to review the changes and merge (combine) them into the main branch. Only reviewed, merged work on the main branch is what gets released. This solves the problem directly: anyone can see exactly which version is in production, and a bad change can be rolled back by returning to an earlier commit. A common mistake is to keep configuration files outside the repository; then settings drift between servers with no history of who changed what.

CI stands for continuous integration: every change is merged into the shared code often, and each merge automatically triggers a build and tests so problems are caught within minutes. CD stands for continuous delivery or continuous deployment: after the tests pass, the software is automatically packaged and made ready for release (delivery), or pushed all the way to production automatically (deployment). A pipeline is the ordered list of automated steps that carry a change from the repository toward production. Jenkins is an automation server, a program that watches the repository and runs those steps for you. A sensible order: first, Jenkins detects the merge to the main branch and checks out (downloads) that exact version of the code. Second, build: compile or package the application. Third, test: run the automated tests; if any fail, the pipeline stops and alerts the team, and nothing is deployed. Fourth, package the result as a versioned artifact (the finished, deployable bundle) and store it. Fifth, deploy to a staging environment (a copy of production used for checking) and run further checks. Sixth, deploy to production, either automatically or after an approval step. The key point a grader should look for is that tests run before any deployment and a failure halts the pipeline. A common mistake is putting deployment before testing, which ships broken code to customers.

Ansible is a configuration management and automation tool: you describe the desired state of your servers in a file, and Ansible connects to each server and makes it match. The list of servers it manages is called an inventory, and the file describing the tasks and desired state is called a playbook. Dana would add all 14 machines to the inventory, write a playbook stating that the configuration file must contain the new payment service address, store the playbook in the Git repository, and run it once. Ansible applies the same change to every machine in the inventory, so no machine is skipped, which was the exact cause of the outage. Idempotent means that running the same operation many times gives the same result as running it once. An Ansible task that says the file should contain this value will change a machine that is wrong and leave alone a machine that is already correct. This matters because the playbook can be run again safely at any time, for example after adding new servers or to check for drift, without breaking machines that were already right. A common mistake is writing tasks that append a line every time they run, which is not idempotent and would duplicate the setting on each run.

An event-driven design is one where work starts automatically in response to an event, which is a record that something happened, such as a file being uploaded, a message arriving or an order being placed. Here, the event is a customer photo landing in the cloud storage area where uploads are saved. The storage service is set to emit an event on each new upload. That event triggers a small piece of code, for example a serverless function, meaning code the cloud provider runs on demand without you managing a server, or it places a message on a managed queue that a worker reads from. The function reads the new photo, creates the thumbnail and saves it. Trace one upload: the customer uploads a photo, storage records it and emits an event, the function starts, the thumbnail is written, and it appears within seconds. This is better than the nightly script because it does not depend on one person's laptop being switched on, it handles each photo as soon as it arrives instead of up to a day later, and it scales with demand, since busy days simply trigger more runs. A common mistake is to replace the laptop with a server that checks for new photos every few minutes; that still adds delay and wastes resources compared with reacting to the event itself.
